physical-1-k3.a: No; ESRM is not convergence and works with any structure.

physical-1-k4.q: How does ERM differ from ESRM?
physical-1-k4.a: ERM covers all key risks (financial, operational, strategic); ESRM covers security risks. ESRM can be a subcomponent of ERM or stand alone.

physical-1-k5.q: What are the three components of ESRM?

physical-1-k6.q: What are the four processes of the ESRM Cycle?
physical-1-k6.a: Identify and prioritize assets; identify and prioritize risks; mitigate prioritized risks; continuous improvement.

physical-1-k7.q: By what criterion are assets prioritized?
physical-1-k7.a: By their criticality to the organization's mission and strategy.

physical-1-k8.q: Does senior management include the CSO?
physical-1-k8.a: No; it sits above the security leader and does not include that role.

physical-1-k9.q: Who approves the controls and who executes the plan?
physical-1-k9.a: The asset owner approves; the security professional executes.

physical-1-k10.q: Which security functions contribute most to continuous improvement?
physical-1-k10.a: Incident response, investigations and analysis, and information sharing.

physical-1-k11.q: What are the four components of the Foundation?
physical-1-k11.a: Holistic risk management, stakeholder partnership, transparency, and governance.

physical-1-k12.q: What three operating environments must security understand?

physical-1-k14.q: Who should make up the majority of the ESRM governance body?
physical-1-k14.a: Security risk stakeholders, not security professionals.

physical-1-k15.q: Which governance document uses "should/may" and which uses "shall/must"?

physical-2-k0.q: What is the basic purpose of physical security?
physical-2-k0.a: To protect tangible, intangible, or mixed assets: people, property, or information.

physical-2-k1.q: Which definition of physical security mentions espionage, sabotage, damage, and theft?
physical-2-k1.a: The one from the U.S. Department of Homeland Security (DHS).

physical-2-k2.a: The condition of being protected against hazards, threats, risks, tampering, or loss.

physical-2-k4.q: What are the seven functions of physical security?
physical-2-k4.a: Access control, deterrence, detection, assessment, delay, response, and evidence gathering.

physical-2-k5.q: Which function is the hardest to measure?

physical-2-k6.q: Why is detection alone of little value?
physical-2-k6.a: Because false positives depend on the system's sensitivity.

physical-2-k7.q: Which function determines what was detected and whether a response is initiated?

physical-2-k8.q: According to Figure 2.1, which measure covers all the columns?

physical-2-k9.q: Which lock does the book recommend if there are windows next to the door?

physical-2-k10.a: It enhances other components and can reduce more expensive physical measures.

physical-2-k11.q: What three elements does an IDS usually have?
physical-2-k11.a: Sensors; alarms or annunciators; and a communication or transmission mechanism.

physical-2-k12.q: What other names are used for security operations centers?

physical-2-k13.q: Why does the dual use of the credential require coordinating physical and IT security?
physical-2-k13.a: Because the same credential grants physical access and logical access.

physical-2-k14.q: What is a major challenge with peripherals during construction or renovations?
physical-2-k14.a: The conflict between security systems and life safety systems.

physical-3-k0.q: What does a security survey emphasize more than a full risk assessment does?
physical-3-k0.a: Vulnerabilities; the risk assessment weighs assets, threats, vulnerabilities, and consequences equally.

physical-3-k1.q: What are the four purposes of a security survey?
physical-3-k1.a: To document the current posture, identify deficiencies and excesses, compare it with the level needed, and recommend improvements.

physical-3-k2.q: Who gave the classic definition of a security survey cited by Broder (2012)?

physical-3-k3.q: In K = Cp + Ct + Cr + Ci – I, what is I and how does it enter the formula?
physical-3-k3.a: The available insurance or indemnity; it is subtracted.

physical-3-k4.q: How does the book define an asset's criticality?
physical-3-k4.a: The impact of its loss, measured in monetary terms.

physical-3-k5.q: In Risk = (T × V × I)^1/3, what scale does each factor use and what is the cube root for?
physical-3-k5.a: 0 to 100; the root returns the result to the 0–100 scale.

physical-3-k6.q: With that formula, if vulnerability is 0, what is the risk?
physical-3-k6.a: Zero (at that time and place), because the factors are multiplied.

physical-3-k7.q: What two attributes are commonly used to measure a vulnerability?

physical-3-k8.q: For natural threats, what does observability mean?
physical-3-k8.a: The ability of security personnel to detect and track the approaching threat (early warning).

physical-3-k9.q: Which threats and vulnerabilities are the hardest to identify and measure?

physical-3-k10.q: What role does the team take on in the outside-inward methodology?
physical-3-k10.a: The adversary's; it is a penetration test from the outside in toward the asset.

physical-3-k11.q: In inside-outward, what example of interdependence does the book give?
physical-3-k11.a: The effect of a power outage, or how many layers an intruder with a stolen master key could get through.

physical-3-k12.q: What are the five criteria of a good report according to Broder (2012)?
physical-3-k12.a: Accuracy, clarity, conciseness, timeliness, and slant or pitch.

physical-3-k13.q: Who is responsible for mitigation and owns the plan?
physical-3-k13.a: The risk owner; the security team advises and supports.

physical-3-k14.q: When are automated assessment tools most useful?
physical-3-k14.a: In low-risk scenarios, or when the assessor knows little and is looking for a best-practices baseline.

physical-4-k0.q: According to Rathburn (2009), what is a metric?
physical-4-k0.a: A measurement against a reference with at least two points (e.g., quantity over time).

physical-4-k1.q: What risk do Williams and Schultz (2016) point out?
physical-4-k1.a: Executing a bad process well: brilliant metrics on a broken process (17,000 viruses cleaned, 5,000 undetected).

physical-4-k2.q: What are the three groups of Security MET criteria, and how many criteria are there in total?

physical-4-k3.q: What does a low score on the Security MET worksheet indicate?
physical-4-k3.a: Where the metric has room for improvement.

physical-4-k4.q: What do the R and the T stand for in Payne's (2006) SMART?

physical-4-k5.q: What test must a metric pass so it is not just noise?
physical-4-k5.a: The who cares? test: there must be a consumer with a defined need (Rathburn, 2009).

physical-4-k6.q: What are the three ideas of the Enterprise Performance Framework (Frost, 2007)?

physical-4-k7.q: What are the three components of a physical security program for metrics purposes?

physical-4-k8.q: What are systems metrics aiming for in the SOC?
physical-4-k8.a: Reducing noise so that only legitimate alarms come through.

physical-4-k9.q: After card-out exit was removed, every exit through the turnstile triggers a door forced alarm. Cause?
physical-4-k9.a: The system was not programmed for free egress mode.

physical-4-k10.q: In the example, what reduced the door held open alarms?
physical-4-k10.a: Programming the alarm to trigger only after 15 minutes.

physical-4-k11.q: In a contract surveillance plan, who measures the guard force's response, and with what?
physical-4-k11.a: The COR, with a stopwatch (e.g., by activating a duress alarm).

physical-4-k12.q: A security officer completed 9 of 15 required courses. Compliance rate?

physical-4-k13.q: What does MTTMV measure, and in what units?
physical-4-k13.a: The mean time to mitigate known vulnerabilities; in units of time.

physical-4-k14.q: Stable system with few failures: which maintenance contract is best?
physical-4-k14.a: Time and materials; with a high failure rate, fixed price.

physical-5-k0.q: What are the two foundational principles of physical security design?
physical-5-k0.a: The 4 Ds (deter, detect, delay, deny) and defense-in-depth.

physical-5-k1.q: According to the book, what is the critical detection point?
physical-5-k1.a: The point where the remaining delay exceeds the response force time.

physical-5-k2.q: What is the difference between area security and point security?
physical-5-k2.a: Area: strong perimeter and strict entry at a single access point. Point: loose perimeter and focus on buildings or restricted areas.

physical-5-k3.q: What does the choice between point and area security depend on?
physical-5-k3.a: The nature of the threat; the usual answer is a bit of both.

physical-5-k4.q: According to the ASIS PAP 2021 standard, what is done before choosing measures?

physical-5-k5.a: Equal minimum penetration time or difficulty and equal probability of detection at each barrier.

physical-5-k6.q: What usually determines whether an electronic lock is fail safe or fail secure?

physical-5-k7.q: Why avoid feature-based criteria in standards?
physical-5-k7.a: They lead to checklists; what matters is overall performance, not the presence of components.

physical-5-k8.a: Comparing the baseline and upgraded systems, quantifying the improvement, and performing cost-benefit analysis.

physical-5-k9.q: Which performance measure corresponds to delay?
physical-5-k9.a: The time to defeat the obstacles.

physical-5-k10.q: When a component fails, what is more important than knowing its cause?
physical-5-k10.a: Having contingency plans to maintain operations or the security level for a specified time.

physical-5-k11.q: What two types of investigation does the book mention as a procedural tool?

physical-5-k12.a: Lack of coordination with the neighbor: bollards across half an entrance that the attacker goes around.

physical-5-k13.q: What does the attacker who continued on foot with explosives teach?
physical-5-k13.a: A vehicle barrier may not stop a pedestrian; scenarios must be thought through holistically.

physical-5-k14.q: What principle does Vellani (2007) sum up?
physical-5-k14.a: Fit the product to the need, not the need to the product.

physical-6-k0.q: What assets other than a building does the book mention?
physical-6-k0.a: A person, intellectual property, an event, a vehicle, data, a high-value object, living beings, and a capability.

physical-6-k1.q: What three questions guide protection based on the type of asset?
physical-6-k1.a: Mobile measures? Adaptable or static? Constant or variable threat?

physical-6-k2.q: Why is it better to deal with the owner rather than a tenant?
physical-6-k2.a: It gives more negotiating power and more flexibility to modify the structure and to contract.

physical-6-k3.q: What does a multi-tenant building require?
physical-6-k3.a: A more adaptable design over the entire life of the facility.

physical-6-k4.q: What does the case of the two U.S. agencies teach?
physical-6-k4.a: Removing and reinstalling the same equipment creates great cost, waste, and delays.

physical-6-k5.q: Name three elements that depend on the facility's purpose.
physical-6-k5.a: Access control, standoff, sensor types, the guard force, or reliance on utilities.

physical-6-k6.q: What types of intended access does the book distinguish?

physical-6-k7.q: What does the museum case teach?
physical-6-k7.a: A neighbor's incident can cut off the only access route to your own facility.

physical-6-k8.q: Why does a rural or remote location matter?
physical-6-k8.a: Response time is longer, which demands more self-sufficiency.

physical-6-k9.q: What is the biggest predictor of business continuity planning success?

physical-6-k10.q: What are the five general categories of security options?
physical-6-k10.a: Architectural enhancements, systems, policies and procedures, management practices, and security personnel.

physical-6-k11.q: How is the financial risk of loss transferred?
physical-6-k11.a: Through insurance or contractual terms, such as indemnification clauses.

physical-6-k12.q: Which treatment option is always available?
physical-6-k12.a: Accepting the risk as a cost of doing business.

physical-6-k13.q: What four criteria are used to evaluate a mitigation option?
physical-6-k13.a: Availability, affordability, feasibility, and risk acceptance.

physical-6-k14.q: According to its guiding principle, what should a continuity plan contain?
physical-6-k14.a: A risk assessment and a business impact analysis, with the flexibility to adapt.

physical-8-k0.q: What are the chapter's four levels of integration?
physical-8-k0.a: Integrated electronic systems, integrated physical security elements, integrated security programs, and integration into enterprise risk management.

physical-8-k1.q: Which backbone network is preferable for security systems?
physical-8-k1.a: One that is independent of the enterprise network.

physical-8-k2.q: What problems come with using the enterprise network?
physical-8-k2.a: Bandwidth limits, traffic spikes, and permission difficulties.

physical-8-k3.q: What is the advantage of a single source for maintenance?
physical-8-k3.a: It is the single point of contact: it diagnoses and manages the solution.

physical-8-k4.a: A third party that supplies or maintains specific system components.

physical-8-k5.q: What are the three general categories of physical security elements?
physical-8-k5.a: Electronic systems, structural measures, and human capital.

physical-8-k6.q: What factors is the physical security strategy tailored to?
physical-8-k6.a: The facility's mission, nature, location, and threat profile.

physical-8-k7.q: What three primary elements does a successful design integrate?
physical-8-k7.a: Architectural aspects, security systems, and operational factors.

physical-8-k8.a: No; it is a force multiplier and provides cross-checks.

physical-8-k9.q: When should operating procedures for each threat level be defined?
physical-8-k9.a: Before the systems are purchased or installed.

physical-8-k10.q: When is the human element integrated?
physical-8-k10.a: In the design phase, not afterward.

physical-8-k11.q: How do ERM and ESRM differ?
physical-8-k11.a: ERM covers all key risks; ESRM covers security risks and can operate with or without ERM.

physical-8-k12.q: What foundations is ESRM built on?
physical-8-k12.a: Holistic risk management, transparency, governance, and stakeholder partnership.

physical-8-k13.q: Put the integration chain in order.
physical-8-k13.a: Components → electronic system → physical security → security program → ERM.

physical-8-k14.q: What example does the book give of physical security within ERM?
physical-8-k14.a: Liability for robberies at or near ATMs at a financial institution.

physical-9-k0.q: Which provides more delay: two walls in series or a single wall of the same total thickness?
physical-9-k0.a: Two in series: they force the effort to be repeated and the tools to be passed through each wall.

physical-9-k1.q: How far from the roof should the optimal secondary barrier be placed?

physical-9-k2.q: What are the two categories of vehicle barriers, and where does each go?

physical-9-k3.q: Which ASTM rating is equivalent to the Department of State K12?

physical-9-k4.q: What is the absolute maximum height of a bollard?
physical-9-k4.a: 38 in (≈1 m) including the cover; the typical height is 30 in or less.

physical-9-k5.q: Why is a Jersey barrier resting on the ground ineffective?
physical-9-k5.a: Its mass is not enough: it must be embedded and anchored with vertical reinforcing steel.

physical-9-k6.q: What does the UL 350-4 label mean?
physical-9-k6.a: With the exterior at 1,700 °F, the interior stays below 350 °F for at least 4 hours.

physical-9-k7.q: Below what weight does UL require a safe to be anchored?

physical-9-k8.q: Which UL class protects magnetic media, and with what limits?
physical-9-k8.a: Class 150: interior below 150 °F and relative humidity up to 80%.

physical-9-k9.q: What minimum thickness does a cast-in-place concrete vault need?
physical-9-k9.a: 12 in for walls, ceiling, and floor, with additional detection.

physical-9-k10.q: Which electrified lock is inherently fail safe?
physical-9-k10.a: The electromagnetic lock (Maglock): when power is cut, it releases the armature.

physical-9-k11.q: How many theoretical combinations does a 4-wheel padlock with 100 positions have?

physical-9-k12.q: What are the three security problems with master keying?
physical-9-k12.a: Control of the master keys, more shear lines for surreptitious opening, and more maintenance.

physical-9-k13.q: What reflected light levels does the rule of thumb recommend for detection, recognition, and identification?

physical-10-k0.q: Who coined the term CPTED (1971), and which work by Oscar Newman (1972) gave rise to it?

physical-10-k5.q: What are the 4 strategies of second-generation CPTED (Saville and Cleveland, 2013)?
physical-10-k5.a: Cohesion, capacity threshold, community culture, and connectivity.

physical-10-k6.q: What does third-generation CPTED focus on?
physical-10-k6.a: Environmental sustainability, green technology, and digital media.

physical-10-k10.a: Those larger than 96 sq in (619 cm²) and less than 18 ft (5.5 m) above the ground.

physical-10-k12.a: Metal halide: it lasts about 20,000 h and renders color well.

physical-10-k13.q: What typical minimum lighting is called for at the front of an ATM?

physical-11-k0.q: What unit measures the coercivity of a magnetic stripe, and what range does high coercivity cover?
physical-11-k0.a: The oersted: 2,500–4,000 Oe; credit cards use 300 Oe.

physical-11-k2.q: What is the point where Type I and Type II errors are equal called?
physical-11-k2.a: Equal error rate (EER); it is used for comparison and is not necessarily the operating point.

physical-11-k3.q: Why isn't a traditional magnetometer used to detect contraband?
physical-11-k3.a: It is passive and detects only ferromagnetic metals.

physical-11-k4.q: Which X-ray technique is the only one that calculates mass, density, and absorption coefficient?
physical-11-k4.a: Computed tomography (CT); it is expensive and produces up to 20% nuisance alarms.

physical-11-k5.q: How does a false alarm differ from a nuisance alarm?
physical-11-k5.a: Nuisance: any alarm not caused by an intrusion. False: generated by the equipment itself.

physical-11-k6.q: Two independent sensors with a PD of 0.9 combined with AND: what PD does the system have?
physical-11-k6.a: 0.81; the NAR goes down. With OR, the NARs add up.

physical-11-k7.q: Under the European standard, what grade is a system with grade 3 and grade 2 equipment?
physical-11-k7.a: Grade 2, the grade of the lowest-grade equipment.

physical-11-k8.q: According to UL 634, which switch does a new installation in a SCIF require?
physical-11-k8.a: HSS2; HSS1 (formerly BMS) remains only in an existing, unmodified SCIF.

physical-11-k9.q: In what order are camera criteria chosen?
physical-11-k9.a: Sensitivity, resolution, and features; the camera before the lens.

physical-11-k10.q: How many pixels per foot do facial recognition and license plate reading require?

physical-11-k11.q: Why are fake cameras a legal liability?
physical-11-k11.a: They create an expectation of protection that does not exist.

physical-11-k12.q: What are the two critical elements of an AC&D system?
physical-11-k12.a: Communicating the data and presenting it to the operator in an understandable way.

physical-11-k13.q: What advantage does the McCulloh circuit provide, and when does it fail?

physical-12-k0.q: What five capabilities in the "necessary human being" concept justify placing a person at a post?
physical-12-k0.a: Distinguishing based on complex criteria, interacting face to face, using or threatening force, making decisions in unforeseen situations, and reporting continuously.

physical-12-k1.q: With personal recognition and low traffic, how many entrances can a remote operator control?

physical-12-k2.q: How do the post log and the main/control log differ?
physical-12-k2.a: The post log is chronological and covers a single post; the control log compiles the significant events from all posts.

physical-12-k3.q: In a paper log, what format is used for the time, and how is an error corrected?
physical-12-k3.a: Military time (24 h); the correction goes on a separate line, as a new entry, in ink.

physical-12-k4.q: When should an officer be armed, if regulations permit it?
physical-12-k4.a: When there is greater danger to life without the weapon, or when the officer can reasonably be expected to use deadly force.

physical-12-k5.q: In a bomb threat on one floor, where is a partial evacuation concentrated?
physical-12-k5.a: On the floors immediately above and below.

physical-12-k6.q: For the officer, what is a person with an altered mental state?
physical-12-k6.a: A medical emergency: the officer secures the person and the scene and calls EMS.

physical-12-k7.q: What is the largest cost of contract security, and how is quality protected?
physical-12-k7.a: The officer's wages; through detailed bid specifications (requirements, wages, benefits, performance).

physical-12-k8.q: Which training method originated at Harvard in the 1880s, and what is it used for?
physical-12-k8.a: The case study; for topics requiring discretionary judgment (crises, use of force, ethics).

physical-12-k9.q: What distinguishes a mentor from an FTO?
physical-12-k9.a: The mentor teaches without evaluating; the FTO evaluates and recommends retention or termination.

physical-12-k10.q: What are the three domains of learning, and which one requires periodic repetition?
physical-12-k10.a: Cognitive, affective, and psychomotor; the psychomotor domain.

physical-12-k14.a: The officer does not know them, they are more objective, and they are useful for reaction tests, such as a suspicious package.

physical-A-k0.a: Control of people, vehicles, and materials through security measures applied to a protected area.

physical-A-k1.a: A combination of sensors, controls, and annunciators arranged to detect and report an intrusion or other emergency. Annunciator: a device that signals by sound, light, or other means.

physical-A-k2.a: Anything tangible or intangible that has value to a person or organization: people, property, and information.

physical-A-k3.a: A natural or man-made obstacle to the movement or direction of people, animals, vehicles, or materials.

physical-A-k4.a: A vehicle barrier: a vertical cylinder (almost always steel filled with concrete) anchored in a deep foundation. It stops vehicles while letting pedestrians and bicycles through. It can take ornamental caps or aluminum, iron, or bronze covers over the crash tube.

physical-A-k5.a: The separation between the interior and the exterior of the building. It is the shell that protects the indoor environment and facilitates its climate control. Its design is an architectural and engineering specialty based on building science.

physical-A-k6.a: A device that captures still or moving images. In security, it is part of a video surveillance system.

physical-A-k7.a: CCT (Corrected Color Temperature): measures how warm or cool a light is, in kelvins. The book says: sunlight = 5,000 K; above that, warmer (yellowish); below, cooler (bluish). **Exam note:** this is backwards; the higher the kelvins, the cooler or bluer the light, and the lower, the warmer (outside the book). The usual name is Correlated Color Temperature (outside the book).

physical-A-k9.q: What is a contract security service?
physical-A-k9.a: A company that provides security services to another entity for a fee; typically, security officers.

physical-A-k10.q: What is crime prevention through environmental design (CPTED)?
physical-A-k10.a: Pronounced “sep-ted.” It reduces crime and the fear of crime through the proper design and use of the built environment. It uses organizational, mechanical, and natural methods to control access, enhance natural surveillance, and foster territoriality, supporting legitimate activity.

physical-A-k11.a: An act or omission that violates a law forbidding or commanding it, and that can be punished with penalties.

physical-A-k12.a: A strategy of forming layers of protection for an asset.

physical-A-k13.a: Frustrating an adversary's attempt to engage in behavior that would constitute a security incident.

physical-A-k14.q: What is a design basis threat (DBT)?
physical-A-k14.a: The threat against which the asset is protected and on which the protection system is designed. It is the baseline type and size of threat the building must withstand. It includes the aggressors' tactics and their tools, weapons, and explosives.

physical-A-k15.a: Discovering an attempt, successful or not, to breach a secured physical or logical perimeter. Physical examples: climbing a fence, opening a locked window, entering an area without authorization.

physical-A-k16.a: A device that lets a person under duress call for help without arousing suspicion.

physical-A-k17.a: A noteworthy occurrence; typically a security incident, an alarm, a medical emergency, or something similar.

physical-A-k18.a: One or more buildings or structures and parking areas, related by function and location, that form an operating entity.

physical-A-k19.q: What is an intrusion detection system?
physical-A-k19.a: A system with one or more sensors that detects an imminent or actual breach (physical or logical). It initiates an alarm, a notification, or a response.

physical-A-k20.a: A manufactured light source: the filament or arc tube, its glass envelope, and its electrical connectors.

physical-A-k21.a: The concentration of light over an area. It is measured in lux (lumens per square meter) or foot-candles (lumens per square foot).

physical-A-k22.a: Degree of illumination. Also, the interior or exterior equipment used to increase it (measured in lux or foot-candles).

physical-A-k23.a: Equipment that prevents an opening from being opened without authorization (gate, window, building door, vault door; not an exhaustive list) and allows authorized users to open it.

physical-A-k24.a: A complete lighting unit: lamp, lampholder, and the reflectors and diffusers that distribute and focus the light.

physical-A-k25.a: Measurements with a reference and at least two points (e.g., quantity over time) that provide insight into performance, operations, or quality.

physical-A-k26.a: Safeguarding a physical or logical boundary or border.

physical-A-k27.a: The part of security that uses physical measures to safeguard, protect, or prevent unauthorized access to assets. Assets: facilities, equipment, people, intangibles, data, and other property.

physical-A-k28.q: What is a physical security assessment?

physical-A-k29.q: What is physical security information management (PSIM)?
physical-A-k29.a: A software platform that integrates unconnected security applications and devices (video, access control, sensors, analytics, networks, building systems; not an exhaustive list) and controls them through one comprehensive interface. It collects and correlates events from disparate systems to identify and resolve situations proactively.

physical-A-k30.q: What is a physical security measure?
physical-A-k30.a: A tangible device, system, or practice to protect people and prevent damage, loss, or unauthorized access to assets.

physical-A-k31.a: A general statement of a principle according to which the organization performs its business functions.

physical-A-k32.a: A nongovernmental, private-sector practice: protecting people, property, and information, conducting investigations, and safeguarding assets. It is performed by an in-house department (proprietary security) or an outside provider (contract security).

physical-A-k33.q: What is a private security officer?
physical-A-k33.a: A person, uniformed or in plain clothes, employed by an organization to protect assets. Formerly often called a “guard.”

physical-A-k34.a: Detailed instructions for implementing policies (security, organizational, or other) or a business practice of a specific function.

physical-A-k35.a: The failure of a primary structural element causes adjacent elements to fail, and those cause others to fail. The damage spreads until the building partially or totally collapses.

physical-A-k36.q: What is a proprietary security organization?
physical-A-k36.a: Typically, a company department that provides security services to the company itself.

physical-A-k37.a: The likelihood or potential that a threat will exploit vulnerabilities and cause loss of or damage to an asset.

physical-A-k38.a: A systematic process: identifying and valuing assets, listing credible threats, documenting vulnerabilities, describing the impacts of a loss event, and analyzing the risks qualitatively or quantitatively. Risks are reported by priority or severity, with a risk level.

physical-A-k39.a: A business discipline that identifies, analyzes, and communicates risk. It then accepts, avoids, transfers, or controls it to an acceptable level, weighing costs and benefits.

physical-A-k40.a: A description or representation of the risks to an asset, system, geographic area, or other entity, considering situational and influencing factors.

physical-A-k41.a: An undesired occurrence or action that is likely to affect assets.

physical-A-k42.a: A practice or device to protect people and prevent damage, loss, or unauthorized access to equipment, facilities, material, and information.

physical-A-k43.a: A person, uniformed or in plain clothes, employed to protect assets.

physical-A-k44.q: What is a security survey (physical security assessment)?
physical-A-k44.a: A critical on-site examination of a building or facility. It seeks to determine its security status, find deficiencies or excesses, establish the protection needed, and recommend improvements. Data: interviews, observation, and document review.

physical-A-k45.a: An electronic device that measures a physical quantity (temperature, pressure, or sound intensity) and converts it into an electronic signal.

physical-A-k46.a: Applying reinforcement measures to make a site more difficult to penetrate.

physical-A-k47.a: The distance between the asset and the threat, typically for an explosive threat.

physical-A-k48.a: Observation of a place, an activity, or a person.

physical-A-k49.a: Following closely behind a person or vehicle. In access control: attempting to enter a controlled area right behind an authorized person.

physical-A-k50.a: Any entity or action that could cause a loss event, adverse impact, or other harm. It includes threat actors (e.g., a terrorist) and threat actions (e.g., a bombing).

physical-A-k51.a: Any path for carrying out a threat action: a physical route, a sequence of events, or a logical route (through cyber infrastructure).

physical-A-k52.a: The average rate of flow of people, vehicles, objects, or data through an access point, system, or process.

physical-A-k53.a: An electronically encoded device (smart card, electronic key fob, USB device; not an exhaustive list) containing data to authenticate the user's identity. It is used for access control to facilities or to IT equipment.

physical-A-k54.q: What is an uninterruptible power supply (UPS)?
physical-A-k54.a: A system that provides continuous power to an alternating current (AC) line within tolerances. It protects against overvoltage, loss of main power, and intermittent brownouts. It is often used with an emergency generator.

physical-A-k55.a: A room or area of special construction that limits access and protects assets (e.g., against forced entry or fire).

physical-A-k56.a: Computer processing of surveillance video for automated tasks: detecting events in real time, recognizing activities, searching for items (faces, license plates, objects), or extracting data from recorded video.

physical-A-k57.q: What is a video management system (VMS)?
physical-A-k57.a: Software that manages video surveillance system functions: network storage, transmission, camera control, alerts, and IP (Internet protocol) interface.

physical-A-k58.a: A system that captures images and transmits them, typically to monitors, recorders, and control equipment. It includes CCTV and network video systems.

physical-A-k59.a: A weakness, condition, or organizational practice that facilitates or allows a threat (intentional, natural, or inadvertent) to cause harm, or that magnifies a loss event.

physical-C-k2.a: Consensus, openness, due process, and transparency.

physical-C-k4.a: A voluntary standard incorporated into laws, or one that is voluntary in theory but mandatory in practice (e.g., because of insurers or contracts).

physical-C-k7.a: Standardize the solutions that work, review problems, and define new ones; the cycle starts again.

ideas.physical-1: Enterprise Security Risk Management (ESRM) is now the foundation of security management. It replaces the "program-based" approach with a risk management process. The asset owner makes decisions about risk; the security professional advises as a trusted partner.
ideas.physical-2: Physical security protects assets (people, property, and information) with physical measures. Its conceptual basis is the 4 Ds (deter, detect, delay, deny), and it is carried out through seven combined functions. Measures are chosen from a menu, stacked in layers, and coordinated with peripheral systems.
ideas.physical-3: No physical security project should begin without understanding the risk: assets, threats, and vulnerabilities. The basic tool is the risk assessment or the security survey (or physical security assessment). The chapter provides a general risk assessment framework and a more specific one for the physical security survey: methodologies, areas to review, testing, the report, and automated tools.
ideas.physical-4: Metrics turn the physical security program into data that can be compared over time. They show status, trends, and return on investment (ROI) to management. They are useful only if they measure a sound process, have an interested consumer, and are planned before data is collected.
ideas.physical-5: Every physical security project should apply risk management and a set of basic design principles from the planning stage. The two pillars are the 4 Ds and defense-in-depth. The chapter adds concepts (point vs. area, avoiding conflicts, balance, design criteria, procedures) and cases of good and bad practice.
ideas.physical-6: Many factors determine whether a physical security strategy is appropriate, effective, and cost-effective. The team must analyze them at the outset and throughout the project: the asset, the building, the environment, the location, and others (management support, budget, vendors, integration). The chosen mitigation must fit the mission, the risk profile, and operations.
ideas.physical-7: Security is built into the design from the start of the project, not added at the end. Everything begins with the risk assessment and the *design basis threat* (DBT). The site, structure, materials, utilities, and *life safety* systems must work together and in layers.
ideas.physical-8: “Integrated” and “integration” are used with different meanings in the profession. The chapter organizes them into four levels, each broader than the one before. It goes from electronic systems up to enterprise-wide risk management (ERM and ESRM).
ideas.physical-9: Physical security has three components that must work in coordination: structural security, electronic security systems, and the human element (security officers and response forces). This chapter covers the structural part: barriers (9.1), containers and vaults (9.2), locks (9.3), and lighting (9.4). Each structural element is a layer that provides delay, and the weakest part sets the value of the whole.
ideas.physical-10: CPTED (Crime Prevention Through Environmental Design) uses the design and use of the built environment to reduce crime and the fear of crime. It rests on three elements: territoriality, surveillance, and access control, applied through natural, mechanical, and organizational means. It is cheaper to integrate it from the planning stage and to combine it with traditional security.
ideas.physical-11: Electronic systems decide who gets in, detect what should not come in or go out, and warn of intrusions. They then make it possible to view, assess, and communicate alarms so that response is timely. The chapter closes with the integration of all these subsystems and their trends.
ideas.physical-12: Despite the rise of technology, the security officer is still an essential part of integrated asset protection; the key is to combine people, processes, and technology. The chapter covers when personnel are needed, which force model to use, their functions and roles, uniforms and weapons, selection, training, managing the force (orders, schedules, supervision, evaluation), and how to make the most of the human element.
ideas.physical-13: A project is a temporary endeavor, with a start and an end, constrained by scope, schedule, budget, and quality. The security project manager must balance those constraints and base every project on a risk analysis. The chapter presents the typical process for an integrated physical protection system project, from concept to the 12-month warranty.
ideas.physical-14: Designing a security system is a sequential process: risk analysis, requirements, basis of design, and conceptual design; then design and documentation (specifications, drawings, schedules), cost estimating, contracting, and the consultant's role. The chapter then covers video systems (from analog to digital, megapixel, and analytics), integration of legacy systems (access control, video, intercom, and networks), and procurement (forms and process).
ideas.physical-15: Implementation of a *Physical Protection System* (PPS) begins right after the contractor is selected. It has five steps, from site preparation to personnel training. The client controls each phase through reports, tests, and written permissions before accepting the system.
ideas.physical-16: Many security systems fail simply because of poor maintenance. Maintenance is planned from the design stage and budgeted from the time of purchase. A successful program has three elements: maintenance, evaluation, and replacement.
ideas.physical-B: A high-rise building exceeds the reach of fire department equipment, so fires are fought from inside. It concentrates people and property and cannot be evacuated all at once. Protecting it requires balancing life safety, which is mandated by codes, with physical security, which sometimes pursues the opposite.
ideas.physical-C: A standard is a set of criteria, guidelines, and best practices that improves the quality and reliability of products, services, or processes. There are voluntary standards, standards mandated by law, and hybrid standards.

physical-1-q0.q: In an ESRM (Enterprise Security Risk Management) cycle, the security director has identified a prioritized risk to the data center and recommended three possible controls. The data center operations manager, who is directly responsible for its successful operation, must choose. Who holds the final decision on mitigation?
o: The operations manager, as the asset owner
The security director, as the subject matter expert
Top management, which sits above the CSO
The security governance body, which sets risk policy
physical-1-q0.e: In ESRM the asset owner is the risk owner: he or she decides on and approves the controls. The security professional recommends, documents, and executes the plan, but does not decide for the owner.

physical-1-q1.q: According to the book, which of the following statements about ESRM is CORRECT?
o: It can work with different leaders for physical and information security
It requires the convergence of physical security and cybersecurity under one leader
It is equivalent to ERM, since it covers financial, operational, and strategic risks
It can only be implemented if the organization has a formal ERM function
physical-1-q1.e: ESRM is not convergence: it manages risk under any structure, and convergence is not indispensable. Nor is it ERM (Enterprise Risk Management), which covers all key risks; ESRM is an independent system that works with or without ERM.

physical-1-q2.q: A newly hired security director wants to adopt ESRM in a hospital chain. According to the book, what is usually the FIRST step when adopting this approach?
o: Reinforce his or her knowledge of the organization's mission and vision
Draft the security risk management plan with each asset owner
Identify and prioritize risks by their potential to impact the mission
Write the standards and procedures for the security governance body
physical-1-q2.e: Understanding the organization is an initial step in the Context of ESRM; mission and vision are the top of the strategy, and reinforcing this knowledge is usually the first step. Identifying and prioritizing risks belongs to the Cycle and comes after prioritizing assets.

physical-1-q3.q: When studying the operating environment, a security professional analyzes the intensity of competition, the company's growth phase, and the speed of decision-making. What type of environment is being assessed?
o: The nonphysical environment
The physical environment
The logical environment
The organizational governance environment
physical-1-q3.e: The nonphysical environment includes the geopolitical environment, industry pressures, legal requirements, competition, growth phase, and speed of decision-making. The physical environment covers location, building, traffic, and on-site processes; the logical one covers information, digital assets, and networks.

physical-1-q4.q: To obtain budget, a security manager presents the asset owner with only worst-case scenarios, without metrics, in order to create alarm. Which concept of the ESRM Foundation is he MOST directly violating?
o: Risk transparency
Process transparency
Holistic risk management
ESRM governance
physical-1-q4.e: Risk transparency requires presenting risks as they are, neither exaggerated nor minimized, using objective statements and quantifiable metrics; the book calls for measured risk rather than fear, uncertainty, and doubt. Process transparency concerns stakeholders understanding the steps of risk management, not how the risk is sized.

physical-1-q5.q: A tactical security document recommends that contractors 'should' be escorted in operational areas and 'may' use the general cafeteria. What type of governance document is it MOST likely to be?
o: A guideline
A standard
A policy
A procedure
physical-1-q5.e: Guidelines are tactical documents like standards, but less rigid: they recommend what 'should/may' be done. Standards set what 'shall/must' be done; policies are high-level, and procedures give step-by-step instructions.

physical-2-q0.q: At 2:00 a.m., a perimeter sensor activates. The control center operator reviews the corresponding camera to determine whether it is an animal or an intruder and to decide whether to dispatch a patrol. Which physical security function is the operator performing?
o: Assessment
Detection
Response
Access control
physical-2-q0.e: Assessment is the system's ability to determine what was detected and decide whether to initiate a response. Detection already occurred when the sensor activated (perceiving a possible intruder), and response would be dispatching the patrol to neutralize or contain the event.

physical-2-q1.q: According to the chapter, what must form the conceptual basis of EVERY physical security project?
o: The four Ds: deter, detect, delay, and deny
The seven basic functions, from access control to evidence gathering
Controlling access, observing, detecting events, and responding
Layers of security applied as building blocks
physical-2-q1.e: The book states that the four Ds must be the basis of every project: each measure is valued for its ability to deter, detect, delay, and deny. The seven functions are how the strategy is carried out, not its conceptual basis; the book expressly warns against confusing them.

physical-2-q2.q: Which definition of physical security expressly mentions defending against espionage, sabotage, damage, and theft?
o: The U.S. Department of Homeland Security (DHS) definition
The ASIS Physical Asset Protection (PAP) Standard definition
The definition in the Protection of Assets Physical Security volume
That same volume's definition of 'security'
physical-2-q2.e: Only the DHS definition names espionage, sabotage, damage, and theft. The PAP Standard's speaks of protecting people and preventing unauthorized access to equipment, material, and documents against an incident; the volume's is the same but says 'information' instead of 'documents.'

physical-2-q3.q: During the remodeling of an office building, the proposed access control design locks doors that the life safety systems need for evacuation. According to the book, what is the BEST approach?
o: Rely on standards and codes, and recommend compensating measures within the planning
Keep the design and delegate evacuation to the building's facilities department
Exclude life safety systems from the scope of the physical security project
Postpone the decision until the regular testing performed after the systems are installed
physical-2-q3.e: The book identifies the conflict between security and life safety systems as a major challenge in construction and remodeling; standards and codes usually ease it and, when needed, compensating measures are recommended within the planning. Excluding or postponing the issue contradicts the point that all peripherals deserve close attention in any project.

physical-2-q4.q: During the design phase of a new corporate campus, the CFO questions why CPTED (Crime Prevention Through Environmental Design) should be included from the start. What is the BEST argument according to the book?
o: It acts as a force multiplier and can reduce other, more expensive physical measures
It fully replaces the need for electronic surveillance systems and the security officer force
It is the easiest measure to quantify, so it best justifies the budget
It eliminates conflicts with life safety systems and building controls
physical-2-q4.e: The book calls CPTED a force multiplier: it strengthens the system and can reduce other, often more expensive, physical measures; that is why it should be considered in almost every project and from the start. It does not replace other measures: a site's selection must cover all functions with layered measures.

physical-3-q0.q: A consultant is performing a comprehensive risk assessment. He has already identified the assets, assigned them a value, and assessed the relevant threats. According to the book's sequence, what is the NEXT step?
o: Assess the vulnerabilities
Consider the impact of a loss event
Summarize and prioritize the risks found
Recommend mitigation measures and merge them into a strategy
physical-3-q0.e: The sequence is: assets and value, then threats, then vulnerabilities, then the impact of a loss event, then summarizing and prioritizing, then recommending mitigation. Impact is considered after assessing vulnerabilities, not before.

physical-3-q1.q: A company located in a flood-prone coastal area has never experienced a flood. Its manager proposes rating the likelihood of flooding as low because there is no history. What is MOST correct according to the book?
o: Likelihood is still higher than inland, because the location favors it
Likelihood is low, because the site's historical data is the only valid criterion
Likelihood does not apply, because it is only calculated for manmade threats
Likelihood should be set by the asset owner according to his or her risk appetite
physical-3-q1.e: The book uses this example: a company in a flood-prone or coastal area is more likely to flood than one inland even if it has never flooded, because geographic location is one of the likelihood factors. The site's historical data is only one of several factors.

physical-3-q2.q: A piece of critical equipment is destroyed. Permanent replacement: $50,000; temporary substitute: $5,000; related costs (removing the old one and installing the new one): $3,000; lost income: $12,000; insurance covers $40,000. Using the book's cost-of-loss formula, what is the total cost of loss (K)?
physical-3-q2.e: K = Cp + Ct + Cr + Ci - I = 50,000 + 5,000 + 3,000 + 12,000 - 40,000 = $30,000. Insurance or indemnity (I) is subtracted: ignoring it gives $70,000 and adding it gives $110,000.

physical-3-q3.q: When ranking assets by criticality, an analyst notes that the failure of an electrical substation would stop three other organizational assets from operating. Which of the book's criticality criteria BEST reflects this observation?
o: Dependencies
Service delivery
Workforce
Mission/objectives
physical-3-q3.e: The dependencies criterion measures the asset's importance to other assets of the organization or network. Service delivery measures the percentage of total service delivery that depends on the asset, and mission/objectives combines all factors into an overall importance.

physical-3-q4.q: When assessing a plant's vulnerability to hurricanes using the observability and exploitability approach, what does observability represent?
o: The security staff's ability to detect and track the approaching threat
The adversary's ability to see and identify the plant's vulnerability
The hurricane's ability to damage the facility, mission, or organization
Whether the security staff knows the plant's vulnerabilities in advance
physical-3-q4.e: For natural threats, observability is inverted: it is the security staff's ability to observe, detect, or track the approaching threat, which requires early warning. The natural threat's ability to cause damage corresponds to exploitability.

physical-3-q5.q: An analyst uses the book's formula Risk = (Threat × Vulnerability × Impact)^1/3, with each factor rated 0 to 100. For one scenario he rates threat = 90, impact = 100, and vulnerability = 0, because the asset is not accessible at that time. What is the result?
o: 0, because the factors are multiplied
63.3, the average of the three factors
95, because the highest factors dominate
190, the sum of the three factors
physical-3-q5.e: The formula multiplies rather than adds: if any factor is 0, the risk is 0 at that time and place. The cube root only returns the product to the 0-100 scale; it does not average or add the factors.

physical-3-q6.q: A manager proposes spending $100,000 on equipment to prevent the theft of an item valued at $1,000. According to the book's cost-benefit analysis, what is MOST appropriate?
o: Insure the item or move it to a more secure location
Buy the equipment, since the item's value includes indirect costs
Install the equipment and transfer the remaining risk via an indemnity clause
First conduct an outside-inward penetration test
physical-3-q6.e: The book (Patterson, 2013) uses this example: it makes no sense to spend $100,000 to prevent the theft of a $1,000 item; it is better to insure it or move it to a more secure place. The real cost of a measure must be compared with its projected impact, such as loss reduction.

physical-3-q7.q: What MAINLY distinguishes a security survey from a comprehensive risk assessment?
o: The survey places more emphasis on vulnerabilities
The survey weighs assets, threats, and consequences equally
The survey focuses on the likelihood of loss events
The survey replaces asset valuation with checklists
physical-3-q7.e: The comprehensive assessment focuses equally on assets, threats, vulnerabilities, and consequences; the security survey places more emphasis on vulnerabilities, and its appraisal component consists of developing and communicating recommendations. The book also warns that checklists must not be the center of the survey.

physical-3-q8.q: An assessment team starts at the vault and works toward the perimeter. At each layer it analyzes how the measures operate and asks, for example, how many layers an intruder with a stolen master key would cross before being detected. Which methodology is it applying?
o: Inside-outward
Outside-inward
Functional (security discipline)
Penetration test
physical-3-q8.e: In the inside-outward methodology the team acts as the defender, works from the asset toward the outer perimeter, and analyzes interdependencies at each layer, such as a stolen master key. Outside-inward takes the adversary's role and is itself a penetration test moving from the outside toward the asset.

physical-3-q9.q: A security survey report contains correct data, but takes a 'gotcha' tone that highlights how bad the client's posture is and dwells on minor details. Which of Broder's (2012) criteria for a good report does it MOST directly fail?
o: Slant or pitch
Clarity
Conciseness
Accuracy
physical-3-q9.e: Slant or pitch requires a courteous report, not nitpicking, without a 'gotcha' tone, and focused on how to improve and why it matters. Conciseness refers to the report's length, not its attitude toward the client.

physical-3-q10.q: According to the book, in which situation are automated assessment tools MOST useful?
o: In low-risk scenarios, or to establish a best-practice baseline
In high-risk scenarios where organizational culture and personality weigh heavily
When the goal is to replace the professional in calculating threat, vulnerability, and consequence
When the character or nature of a risk must be assessed, more than its magnitude
physical-3-q10.e: The book says they are useful in low-risk scenarios or when the assessor knows little and wants a best-practice baseline; the key word is 'assist,' and they must not be the only element. Their main problem is that they handle intangible factors poorly, such as the character of a risk or the organization's culture.

physical-4-q0.q: The guard supervisor boasts that his officers completed 100% of the scheduled patrols this quarter. However, the patrol route does not include the parking lot, where most thefts occur. According to Williams and Schultz (2016), what problem does this situation illustrate?
o: Executing a bad process well: good numbers measuring a flawed process
Lack of a baseline, without which totals provide no useful information
A metric that fails the 'who cares?' test
A metric without repeatability, which cannot be compared even with itself
physical-4-q0.e: Williams and Schultz warn of the risk of executing a bad process well: the numbers look good but measure an immature or broken process, like the IT example that cleaned 17,000 viruses and missed 5,000. The lesson is to know what is measured, the quality of the metrics, and what is NOT measured.

physical-4-q1.q: In the ASIS Foundation's Security Metrics Evaluation Tool (Security MET), to which group of criteria do cost, timeliness, and manipulation belong?
o: Operational (security) criteria
Technical criteria
Strategic (corporate) criteria
Behavioral criteria
physical-4-q1.e: The Security MET has 9 criteria in three groups: technical (reliability, validity, generalizability), operational (cost, timeliness, manipulation), and strategic (ROI, organizational relevance, communication). 'Behavioral' refers to the behavioral summary scale that accompanies each criterion, not to a group.

physical-4-q2.q: In Payne's (2006) SMART metrics model used by the book, what do the R and the T stand for?
o: Repeatable and time-dependent
Relevant and time-bound
Reliable and timely
Realistic and trackable
physical-4-q2.e: In Payne's SMART, R = repeatable (produced consistently and uniformly so it can be compared) and T = time-dependent (always collected over the same periods). 'Relevant' and 'time-bound' are not the terms of the model the book presents.

physical-4-q3.q: A security manager wants to distribute to all departments a weekly metric that is only useful to his own team. According to the book, which principle is he overlooking?
o: Collect relevant data: the metric must pass the 'who cares?' test
Start small: a few initial data points show the total effort required
Measurable: the formula must yield a natural number or a percentage
Attainable: if gathering it takes too long, it loses effectiveness
physical-4-q3.e: The collect relevant data principle requires that the information serve someone; some metrics only interest the manager and his team and should not be distributed. Without a consumer with a defined need, the metric only adds noise (Rathburn, 2009).

physical-4-q4.q: By executive decision, a company stops requiring a card to exit through the turnstiles. Since then, every exit generates a forced door alarm in the SOC. What is the MOST likely cause according to the book's example?
o: Free egress mode was not programmed on the turnstiles
The door position switch is misaligned
Users do not hold the card in front of the reader long enough
The bypass time configured for the turnstiles has expired
physical-4-q4.e: In the book's example, card exit was removed but free egress mode was not programmed, so every exit triggered an alarm; once corrected, only the entry side alarmed. Card misreads from not holding the card occur when presenting it to enter and do not explain alarms on every exit.

physical-4-q5.q: In public sector facility compliance, what does the MTTMV (mean time to mitigate vulnerabilities) metric MAINLY indicate?
o: How the organization reacts to detected vulnerabilities, in units of time
The percentage of facilities that currently have a valid security assessment
The average mitigation cost of each audit finding
The number of vulnerabilities identified in each initial assessment
physical-4-q5.e: MTTMV averages, over the mitigated vulnerabilities, the time between detection and mitigation; it shows how the organization reacts and which processes need to be sped up. The percentage of facilities with a current assessment is a different formula, whose goal is 100%.

physical-4-q6.q: A guard services contract requires a maximum alarm response time. According to the book, how is that requirement verified within a contract surveillance plan?
o: The COR triggers an alarm, e.g., a duress alarm, and times the response
The integrator submits a monthly service call report as a deliverable
Employees rate the response in an anonymous satisfaction survey
The SOC calculates the mean time between detection and mitigation of each vulnerability
physical-4-q6.e: For guard force response a stopwatch is enough: the COR (contracting officer representative) triggers an alarm, such as a duress alarm, measures how long the proper response takes, and compares it with the contract requirements. The monthly service call report relates to the systems integrator's response, not the guards'.

physical-4-q7.q: The security office measures how many training needs it identified, how many workplace violence prevention courses it delivered to employees, and what percentage of them attended. What type of metric is it using?
o: Outward-facing training metric
Inward-facing training metric
Response to customer requests metric
Facility compliance metric
physical-4-q7.e: Outward-facing metrics measure the training the security office designs and delivers to employees or other audiences: needs identified, courses developed and delivered, and attendance percentage. Inward-facing metrics measure the training required of the security staff itself.

physical-4-q8.q: The electronic security system (ESS) metrics for a campus show a complex integrated system with a high failure rate. According to the book, which type of maintenance contract is MOST appropriate?
o: Fixed-price
Time-and-material
Earned value
Work order agreement
physical-4-q8.e: The book indicates that a complex integrated system with a high failure rate calls for a fixed-price maintenance contract, while a stable system with few failures calls for a time-and-material contract. Earned value is a project management technique, not a contract type.

physical-5-q0.q: A research campus holding intellectual property and controlled materials operates with a lax perimeter and strong controls at each building. Intelligence warns of a new threat from radical activists against the site. According to the book, what adjustment is MOST appropriate?
o: Shift toward area security: a strong perimeter and strict entry through a single portal
Strengthen point security by adding more readers inside the restricted areas
Keep the current scheme, because point security is sufficient under any conditions
Remove the controls at each building and concentrate them all in the control center
physical-5-q0.e: The choice between point security and area security depends on the nature of the threat: under normal conditions point security may suffice, but in the face of a radical activist threat it is advisable to shift to area security, with a strong perimeter and strict control at a single portal. The usual answer is a bit of both.

physical-5-q1.q: A high school installs magnetometers at its two main entrances, but several secondary entrances are left open or have broken locks. Which dimension of balance described in the book is violated?
o: Balance among access points or methods
Balance among types of measures
Balance among targets or assets
Balance among threats
physical-5-q1.e: Balance among access points requires equivalent protection at all of them; the book uses this high school case as an example of a tightly controlled front door with open back entrances. Balance among types of measures refers to orchestrating electronic, structural, human, and procedural measures, not to the coverage of each entrance.

physical-5-q2.q: An internal perimeter detection standard requires 'installing a motion sensor and a fence-mounted sensor' at all sites. Based on the book's design criteria, what is the BEST criticism?
o: It is a feature criterion that leads to checklists; it should set overall performance
It is a performance criterion, useful only for comparing the current and upgraded systems
It is correct, because a fence-mounted sensor is always the best option for the perimeter
It should require more sensor types to cover each technology's false negatives
physical-5-q2.e: Requiring specific components is a feature criterion: it measures effectiveness by the presence of elements and leads to the checklist method, so it should be avoided in standards. The book prefers performance criteria, e.g., 'detect a running intruder using any attack method'; although the book calls the fence sensor 'the best,' performance logic prevails on the exam.

physical-5-q3.q: When planning an electronic security system, the design team discusses how to address component failure. According to the book, what is MOST important?
o: Having contingency plans to maintain operations or the security level for a set time
Identifying the exact cause of each failure before restoring the system
Designing a complex system that will operate its entire service life without failures
Limiting the failure plan to adversary actions that exceed the design threat
physical-5-q3.e: The book says that knowing the cause helps restore the system, but it is more important to have contingency plans that maintain operations or the security level for a set time, e.g., automatic redundant equipment such as generators or batteries. Moreover, a complex system is unlikely to operate its entire life without failures.

physical-5-q4.q: According to this book's definition, what is the critical detection point?
o: The point where the remaining delay time exceeds the response force time
The point where each barrier's probability of detection is exactly equal
The first outer perimeter sensor that detects the adversary's advance
The point where the adversary decides to abort and seek a softer target
physical-5-q4.e: The book defines the critical detection point as the point where the remaining delay exceeds the response force time. Equal penetration time and probability of detection at each barrier describes a balanced system, not this point.

physical-5-q5.q: At a checkpoint, the retractable vehicle barrier prevented a car carrying explosives from tailgating another vehicle inside. The attacker got out with the explosives and ran on foot toward the building while the controller remained focused on the car. What lesson does the book highlight?
o: A vehicle barrier may not stop a pedestrian; scenarios must be considered holistically
The barrier failed in its mission, so it should be replaced with a slower-closing one
The controller should have prioritized the vehicle, since the main threat was the explosive
Bollards should have been installed across half the driveway to increase standoff distance
physical-5-q5.e: The barrier fulfilled its mission but did not stop the attack: a vehicle barrier may not stop a pedestrian, and vice versa. The book calls for thinking outside the box about threats and scenarios and avoiding a piecemeal or silo approach.

physical-6-q0.q: A plant depends on deliveries day and night and has a single access road, which passes a cultural center threatened by hate groups. When reviewing the strategy, which risk does the book MOST emphasize with a similar case?
o: That an incident at the neighbor cuts off the only access route and halts operations
That the neighbor increases the likelihood of shoplifting at the plant's docks
That the cultural center lengthens the response time of local first responders
That the plant inherits legal liability for incidents occurring at the neighbor's site
physical-6-q0.e: In the museum case, a shooter entered the neighboring museum and police cordoned off the neighborhood for several hours, leaving the plant's only transport route inaccessible. Neighbors are almost never chosen, but they must be included in the risk assessment, including their effect on ingress and egress.

physical-6-q1.q: A financial corporation builds a custom building that it will occupy for a few years before selling it, possibly to multiple tenants. According to the book, what security design approach is MOST appropriate?
o: Architectural and security elements that are easy to remove or install
Permanent maximum-security measures tailored only to the corporation
Delay all security measures until the next occupant is known
Delegate security design to each future tenant of the building
physical-6-q1.e: The book cites a corporation that built, occupied for a few years, and sold: its buildings were custom-made but designed for the next occupant, with elements easy to remove or install. The case of the two U.S. agencies shows the opposite mistake: removing and reinstalling the same equipment caused great cost, waste, and delays.

physical-6-q2.q: A company is evaluating locating a distribution center in a remote rural area. According to the book, what security implication must it MAINLY consider because of that location?
o: Longer first responder response times, requiring greater self-reliance
Greater risk of closures from neighbors' incidents on a single access road
Greater need for dual-egress doors under local codes
Less dependence on supporting utilities and infrastructure
physical-6-q2.e: The book notes that, depending on whether the area is dense urban, suburban, or rural or remote, first responder response times vary greatly and may require more self-reliance in an incident; the risk assessment helps determine those needs.

physical-6-q3.q: According to the book, what is the GREATEST predictor of the success or failure of business continuity planning?
o: Senior management commitment
The quality of the business impact analysis (BIA)
The plan's flexibility to adapt to the situation
The relationship with vendors and central stations
physical-6-q3.e: The book states that the greatest predictor of the success or failure of continuity planning is senior management commitment. The risk assessment, the BIA, and flexibility are part of the plan's guiding principle, but are not presented as the greatest predictor.

physical-6-q4.q: According to this chapter, by which four criteria is every mitigation option evaluated for the company's operation?
o: Availability, affordability, feasibility, and risk acceptance
Availability, affordability, feasibility, and risk transfer
Likelihood, impact, feasibility, and risk acceptance
Affordability, effectiveness, legality, and liability
physical-6-q4.e: The chapter evaluates each option by availability, affordability, feasibility, and risk acceptance; it also asks whether the strategy substantially interferes with operations. Risk transfer (insurance or indemnification clauses) is a treatment option, not an evaluation criterion.

physical-7-q0.q: A government client does not share the details of its risk assessment with the designer and provides only the design basis threat (DBT). What information does that document contain?
o: The adversary profile: type, capabilities, tactics, goals, and intent
The codes, standards, and permits applicable to the construction project
The client's acceptable risk levels and mitigation budget
FEMA's classification of natural and human-caused hazards
physical-7-q0.e: The DBT is the adversary profile on which the facility's security engineering and operations are based: type, composition, and capabilities; methods (tactics, techniques, and procedures); and goals, intent, and motivation. Acceptable risk levels are set by the client as part of its assessment, which it may not share.

physical-7-q1.q: In a complex renovation, the architects, engineers, contractor, and security each make design adjustments separately, and no one has a complete view of what has changed. According to the book, what mechanism BEST addresses this situation?
o: A change review board acting as the clearinghouse for all changes
A failure point assessment to determine what will fail first
An updated design basis threat provided by the client to each discipline
Design specifications requiring systems certified through actual testing
physical-7-q1.e: The change review board brings together representatives of each major project partner, and its most important duty is to be the clearinghouse for all changes. Failure point analysis answers what will fail first in a catastrophic event, not how changes are coordinated.

physical-7-q2.q: When designing a plant's perimeter, the team must decide where to place the fence relative to the property line. According to the book's good practice, what is advisable?
o: Slightly inside the property line, for maintenance and boundary visibility
Right on the property line, to gain the maximum standoff distance
Close to the building, so that outside vegetation hides the facility
On the property line with barbed wire, which is enough to stop a determined intruder
physical-7-q2.e: Good practice is not to place the fence right on the property line but slightly inside it: the outer space allows maintenance and boundary visibility, and it prevents neighbors from placing plants or objects that could be used to breach it. Moreover, a standard barbed-wire fence is climbed in seconds: it only 'keeps honest people honest.'

physical-7-q3.q: A site will use color CCTV in its parking lot at night. According to the book, which type of lamp BEST supports color perception for the cameras?
o: Metal halide, because of its white light
High-pressure sodium, because of its yellowish light
Any lamp that maximizes lumens and spillover
Infrared lighting, because it causes no light pollution
physical-7-q3.e: The book indicates that metal halide emits white light and is the best for color CCTV, while high-pressure sodium gives yellowish light. In addition, the design must follow the local code, which seeks to limit light pollution and spillover onto neighboring properties.

physical-7-q4.q: A corporate headquarters is downtown, surrounded by tall buildings. When analyzing the risk of a car bomb, which blast pressure effect MOST aggravates the damage in this urban environment?
o: Reflective pressure
Incendiary thermal effect
Overpressure
Fragmentation
physical-7-q4.e: In urban environments the wave is redirected when it strikes objects, producing multiple impacts from several angles and at different times; reflective pressure can be much stronger than the initial wave at the same distance. The incendiary thermal effect is insignificant unless highly combustible materials are present.

physical-7-q5.q: What BEST describes progressive collapse, and when is it considered, according to the book?
o: A chain failure disproportionate to the initial damage; considered in buildings of 3 or more stories
A chain failure disproportionate to the initial damage; considered only in buildings of 10 or more stories
Facade breakage from reflective pressure; considered in buildings of 3 or more stories
Falling suspended equipment lacking seismic bracing; considered in any building
physical-7-q5.e: Per ASCE/SEI 59-11, progressive collapse is a chain failure of the structural system, disproportionate to the initial local damage (e.g., a blast): one support falls, those above fail, and the building collapses on itself. It is uncommon and is considered in buildings of 3 or more stories.

physical-7-q6.q: In a test based on the GSA window performance conditions table, the glass cracks and its fragments enter and fall to the floor no more than 3.3 ft (1 m) from the window. Which performance condition applies?
o: 3a: high protection, very low hazard
2: very high protection, no hazard
3b: high protection, low hazard
4: medium protection, medium hazard
physical-7-q6.e: In the GSA table, condition 3a describes cracked glass with fragments on the floor no more than 3.3 ft away; 3b extends that distance to 10 ft. In condition 2 the glass cracks but is retained by the frame. Rule: the higher the condition number, the less protection and the more hazard.

physical-7-q7.q: In a retrofit, a client wants to apply blast film to the existing windows on its main facade. According to the book, what must be verified BEFORE considering the issue resolved?
o: That the structure holding the window withstands as much as the reinforced glass
That the film lets in enough natural light to earn LEED points
That the window also has a blast curtain attached to the ceiling and floor
That the original glass is annealed, which is the most resistant type
physical-7-q7.e: When reinforcing glass in a retrofit, the book requires verifying that the structure holding the window can withstand the same load; if it is weaker, it fails and the entire window enters as a large projectile. Standard construction annealed glass fragments easily, so it is not an advantage.

physical-7-q8.q: After several thefts during drills, a plant manager asks that emergency exit doors remain locked during any fire alarm. According to the book, what is the security professional's CORRECT response?
o: Refuse: security cannot override the life safety code, and locks must fail open
Accept it if the doors are alarmed and monitored, with a response to re-secure the area
Accept it if low-mounted photoluminescent signs guide occupants to other exits
Accept it only for doors leading to sensitive, hazardous, or exterior areas of the building
physical-7-q8.e: The golden rule is that security cannot override the life safety code: no lock may prevent an occupant from reaching an exit, and every system must fail open or be failsafe in an emergency. Alarming and monitoring doors to sensitive areas complements that release but does not replace it.

physical-8-q0.q: To save costs, the IT department proposes running the new video surveillance and access control system on the existing enterprise network. According to the book, what is the BEST recommendation?
o: Use an independent network; the enterprise one may limit bandwidth and complicate permissions
Use the enterprise network, since IT will then handle preventive and remedial maintenance
Use the enterprise network, since a dedicated network prevents interoperability between systems
Use an independent network, since it removes the need to coordinate with the IT team
physical-8-q0.e: The book identifies an independent network backbone as the preferred approach; using the enterprise network brings performance problems from limited bandwidth or traffic spikes, as well as permission difficulties. Even so, the key to success is an open, cooperative relationship between the integrator and the IT team, so coordination does not go away.

physical-8-q1.q: In an integrated system, every failure ends in arguments among the camera vendor, the access control vendor, and the network provider over who is responsible. According to the book, which option helps MOST?
o: Assign preventive and remedial maintenance to a single source
Form a stakeholder team to select new interoperable systems
Migrate all security systems to the organization's enterprise network
Replace the vendors with in-house fixed-post and patrol personnel
physical-8-q1.e: The book proposes a single source responsible for preventive and remedial maintenance: as the single point of contact, it diagnoses the cause and manages the solution. A stakeholder team is used to select systems in a renovation or new project, not to settle maintenance responsibility.

physical-8-q2.q: Facing an unexpected absence, the supervisor covers the security operations center (SOC) shift with an officer who is excellent at fixed posts and patrol but has no SOC experience. According to the book, what is the MAIN risk?
o: That he cannot operate or interpret the electronic or building control systems
That his absence reduces the deterrent effect of fixed posts and patrols
That the SOC technology replaces his judgment and removes checks and balances
That the change forces a rewrite of the operating procedures for each threat level
physical-8-q2.e: The book uses this example of a staffing mismatch: an officer who is good at a fixed post or patrol may not be prepared for the SOC, because he may not know how to operate or interpret the systems. The critical point is matching the right person to the role; a mismatch, even one caused by understaffing, can be disastrous.

physical-8-q3.q: A company bought and installed an advanced access control and video system and now plans to write its operating procedures. According to the book, what is the main problem with this sequence?
o: Threat-level procedures should have been set before buying or installing the system
Technology should have replaced staff before any procedures were written
Procedures should only be written after an assessment of the enterprise network
The human element should have been integrated after implementing the system, not before
physical-8-q3.e: The book states that operating procedures for each threat level are defined before buying or installing any system, and that the human element is integrated in the design phase. Installing equipment and software without an operating philosophy can leave systems that increase the risk of harm; moreover, technology is a force multiplier, not a replacement for staff.

physical-8-q4.q: A director coordinates the organization's physical security with personnel security, IT security, investigations, and executive protection. Which level of integration in the chapter BEST describes this work?
o: Integrated security programs
Integrated physical security elements
Integrated electronic security systems
Integration in enterprise risk management
