physical-8-q4.e: The integrated security programs level recognizes that physical security is only one element of the total strategy and integrates it with other disciplines, such as personnel security, IT security, investigations, and executive protection. Integrated physical security elements combine electronic systems, structural measures, and human capital within the physical domain itself.

physical-9-q0.q: A designer has the same total amount of reinforced concrete for the enclosure of a room holding sensitive assets. According to the chapter, which configuration provides the MOST delay against an intruder?
o: Two or more separate walls in series that add up to the same total thickness
A single monolithic wall of the full thickness, which resists more because of its mass
A single full-thickness wall with the rebar spaced farther apart center to center
A single full-thickness wall designed to the structural loads of the building
physical-9-q0.e: Two or more walls in series delay more than a single wall of the same total thickness, because they force the adversary to repeat the effort and carry tools through each wall. Designing a wall only for structural loads is precisely why ordinary reinforced concrete is penetrated quickly, and wider rebar spacing reduces delay rather than increasing it.

physical-9-q1.q: A facility has heavy concrete walls, but its doors are hollow steel with ordinary frames and hinges. Which recommendation BEST reflects the applicable principle from the chapter?
o: Upgrade the door assembly until it matches the delay of the walls, floors and ceilings (balanced design)
Thicken the walls even more, because walls are sometimes the adversary's preferred route for forced entry
Install panic bars so that the doors become one-way barriers against intruders
Replace only the locks, because the lock is what determines the final value of the whole barrier
physical-9-q1.e: The weakest part of a barrier determines its final value, and that part is usually the door; balanced design therefore requires the door, frame, hinges, bolts and lock to provide the same delay as the floors, walls and ceilings. Thickening the walls is pointless while the door remains the weak link: if the door assembly cannot be upgraded enough, upgrading the structure may not even be cost-effective.

physical-9-q2.q: Which type of commercial glass does the chapter identify as preferred against blasts?
o: Laminated: sheets bonded to plastic layers that keep the broken pieces stuck together
Tempered: heat-treated to resist breakage and to break into small pieces when it fails
Wired: its main use is to maintain the fire rating of fire doors and fire windows
Annealed: manufactured to control residual stresses so that it can be cut and worked
physical-9-q2.e: Laminated glass keeps the broken pieces adhered to the plastic interlayers and, installed in a frame anchored to the structure, is the preferred type against blasts. Tempered glass is required by codes because it breaks into small pieces, but it falls in seconds to impact tools; wired glass is used mainly to maintain fire ratings.

physical-9-q3.q: When protecting a utility port, such as a ventilation duct, with steel mesh grilles, where should those covers be placed relative to detection?
o: At the point of detection or after it
Before the point of detection, as far as possible from the sensor
Instead of sensors, since the grille makes detection unnecessary
Only at the outer end of the duct, regardless of where the sensor is
physical-9-q3.e: The chapter states that these covers (grilles, bars, expanded metal mesh) are placed at the point of detection or after it. Because utility ports are hidden routes, they need both barricades and sensors, so a grille does not replace detection.

physical-9-q4.q: The analysis of a warehouse with a metal roof deck with insulation shows that an adversary could enter through the roof. Which upgrade usually offers the BEST value according to the chapter?
o: A secondary barrier below the roof, about 10 to 12 in (25 to 30 cm) beneath it
Reinforcing the roof itself with several inches of rigid insulation over the deck
A secondary barrier below the roof, at least 36 in (0.9 m) beneath it
Replacing the roof with a membrane with embedded mesh over the whole surface
physical-9-q4.e: Upgrades below the roof usually offer the best value: tests suggest that a secondary barrier beneath the roof is more effective than reinforcing the roof itself. The optimal distance is 10 to 12 in, because the small space creates a 'hole effect' and forces a second penetration in a confined space, possibly with different tools.

physical-9-q5.q: During a patrol, a supervisor sees stacked pallets and a dumpster next to the chain link perimeter fence, and tree branches hanging over it. Which deficiency BEST describes what was observed?
o: Failure to maintain the clear zone, one of the most common mistakes
Orienting the top guard inward instead of outward toward the street
Using light, thin-walled posts and rails that weaken the whole fence
Failing to fasten the fabric to the line posts at 15 in (38 cm) intervals
physical-9-q5.e: The clear zone requires removing boxes, ladders, containers, vehicles and equipment next to the fence and pruning overhanging branches, which act as natural ladders. Failing to maintain it is one of the most common mistakes and nullifies the fence's effectiveness; the other options are real defects, but not what was observed.

physical-9-q6.q: At a campus's main vehicle entrance, each authorized vehicle must pass after an officer inspects it. Which blocking barrier is MOST appropriate for that point?
o: Retractable bollards operated from the guard booth
A row of well-anchored engineered planters
Jersey barriers embedded and anchored with reinforcing steel
Fixed bollards with a decorative stainless steel sleeve
physical-9-q6.e: Active (operable) barriers are placed at vehicle access control points and open and close to let authorized vehicles through; the retractable bollard is one of them. Planters, Jersey barriers and fixed bollards are passive barriers: fixed and intended for the perimeter, away from vehicle entrances.

physical-9-q7.q: An architect proposes decorative bollards on the sidewalk of an urban building. According to the chapter's guidelines, which statement about their height is correct?
o: Typically no more than 30 in (0.76 m), and never more than 38 in (about 1 m) including the sleeve
Typically 38 in (about 1 m), with an absolute maximum of 48 in (1.2 m) including the sleeve
They must be 36 to 48 in (0.9 to 1.2 m) tall to resist a vehicle impact
Height is unrestricted as long as the model has been tested by an independent laboratory
physical-9-q7.e: To reduce visual impact, the typical height is no more than 30 in, and in no case should it exceed 38 in, including the decorative sleeve. The 36 to 48 in figure is the recommended spacing between bollards, not their height; independent laboratory testing is required for custom designs but does not remove the height limit.

physical-9-q8.q: After a threat, a manager places concrete Jersey barriers resting on the pavement in front of the entrance, relying on their weight. What is the MOST accurate assessment?
o: They are ineffective that way; they must be embedded and anchored with vertical reinforcing steel
They are effective, because a 12 ft (3.6 m) barrier weighs about 5,700 lb (2,585 kg)
They are effective only if the vehicle strikes at an angle of less than 30 degrees
They are adequate if laid in 12.5 or 20 ft (3.8 or 6 m) sections without any overlaps
physical-9-q8.e: They were believed to protect through their mass, but resting on the ground they are ineffective against a vehicle attack: they must be embedded and anchored with vertical reinforcing steel through the barrier into the pavement. The less-than-30-degree impact angle limit applies to metal highway guard rails, not to Jersey barriers.

physical-9-q9.q: A specification requires a vehicle barrier with a Department of State K12 rating. Which ASTM rating and test condition correspond to it?
o: M50: 15,000 lb (6,800 kg) vehicle at 50 mph (80 km/h)
M40: 15,000 lb (6,800 kg) vehicle at 40 mph (64 km/h)
M30: 15,000 lb (6,800 kg) vehicle at 30 mph (48 km/h)
M50: 12,000 lb (5,440 kg) vehicle at 50 mph (80 km/h)
physical-9-q9.e: In Figure 9.9, K4, K8 and K12 are equivalent to M30, M40 and M50: a 15,000 lb test vehicle at 30, 40 and 50 mph, respectively. M40 corresponds to K8, not K12, and the test vehicle weight is the same in all three ratings.

physical-9-q10.q: A company keeps original paper contracts in a burglary-resistant safe with thick solid steel walls, convinced that it also protects them from fire. What is the MAIN risk?
o: The steel transmits heat quickly to the interior, so the paper is soon destroyed in a fire
The safe's insulation offers little resistance to a hammer blow and is useless against forced entry
The moisture in the insulation evaporates over the years and the safe loses its fire rating
Because it weighs more than 750 lb (340 kg), UL requires anchoring it, so it cannot be removed in an emergency
physical-9-q10.e: A burglary-resistant safe protects with thick solid steel walls, which transmit heat quickly to the interior; in a fire the paper is soon destroyed. Weakness against a hammer and loss of insulation moisture are traits of fire safes, not burglary safes; and UL requires anchoring safes under 750 lb, not over.

physical-9-q11.q: What does the UL label '350-4 Hours' on a fire-resistant safe mean?
o: With the exterior at 1,700 °F (927 °C), the interior does not reach 350 °F (177 °C) for at least 4 hours
With the exterior at 350 °F (177 °C), the paper inside does not char for at least 4 hours
The interior stays below 350 °F (177 °C) and below 80% relative humidity for 4 hours
It resists forced entry for 350 net working minutes and resists fire for 4 hours
physical-9-q11.e: 350 is the maximum interior temperature (at which almost all paper is damaged) and 4 is the number of hours of protection with the exterior at 1,700 °F. The 80% humidity limit belongs to Class 150 for magnetic media; Class 350 allows a maximum of 65%.

physical-9-q12.q: A data center needs to store magnetic backup tapes in a fire-resistant container. Which equipment is MOST appropriate?
o: Class 150 Record Protection Equipment
A Class 350-4 fire-resistant safe, because it protects for more hours than any other class
A Class 350-1 insulated filing device placed in a fire-resistive building
A TL-30 burglary-resistant safe, whose thick steel walls protect the media from heat
physical-9-q12.e: Magnetic media deteriorate from 150 °F (66 °C), and sooner with humidity above 80%, so a container designed for paper is not enough: Class 150 keeps the interior below 150 °F with humidity up to 80%. A 350-4 safe lets the interior rise to 350 °F, a limit intended for paper.

physical-9-q13.q: A client claims that his TL-30 safe guarantees that no burglar can open it in less than 30 minutes. What BEST describes the meaning of that rating?
o: In testing, no one could open the door or make a 6-inch square opening in 30 net minutes
It is the average time a professional safe cracker needs to open that model of safe
The safe withstood 30 minutes of torch and tool attack on all six of its sides
The safe withstood 30 minutes of elapsed clock time, including pauses to change tools
physical-9-q13.e: TL-30 means that the technicians, with the specified tools, could not open the door or make the 6-inch square opening in 30 minutes of net working time: when the tool leaves the safe, the clock stops. It is not the real opening time: any safe can be opened, and a professional safe cracker can do it after several hours, depending on skill.

physical-9-q14.q: What does a UL TRTL-30-X6 rating on a safe for valuables indicate?
o: Torch and tool resistance for 30 minutes of testing on all six sides
Tool resistance for 30 minutes on the door only, against six types of attack
Explosive and tool resistance for 30 minutes of testing on all six sides
Torch resistance for 30 minutes and tool resistance for 6 minutes of testing
physical-9-q14.e: According to Figure 9.19, TR means torch resistant, TL means tool resistant, 30 is the number of test minutes and X6 means the test was performed on all six sides. TR does not refer to explosives: the book attributes explosive resistance to TRTL-60-X6.

physical-9-q15.q: A company builds a vault against forced entry: it installs a heavy door and keeps the existing concrete walls, one of which is an exterior wall. What is the MAIN error?
o: Relying on the walls: all six surfaces must protect equally, and an exterior wall should be avoided
Using reinforced concrete instead of unreinforced concrete, which resists forced penetration better
Not installing a time lock, which by itself prevents any attack through the floor
Locating it above grade, when burglary-resistant vaults must always be in the basement
physical-9-q15.e: All six surfaces of a vault must protect equally; the typical error is to install a heavy door and assume the concrete walls are enough, and an exterior wall gives the intruder a convenient point to attack from outside. Moreover, unreinforced concrete should never be used against forced penetration.

physical-9-q16.q: After changing a vault combination without a locksmith, the custodian wants to verify that the lock was not left set on a single number. What test should be performed?
o: Turn the dial three times to the left, stop at the third number, then turn right to the opening index
Dial the first two numbers and have a second person dial the third and fourth numbers out of sight of anyone else
Turn the dial four times to the right, stop at the first number, then turn left to the opening index
Try fewer than 40 different combinations at random and confirm that none of them retracts the bolt of the door
physical-9-q16.e: The book's test is to turn the dial three times to the left, stop at the third number and turn right to the opening index; if the bolt opens, the combination is on a single number and must be changed immediately. Splitting the 'third and fourth' numbers was precisely the error in the case: the lock had only three numbers, because the opening index is not part of the combination.

physical-9-q17.q: A dial combination lock has 3 wheels with 100 positions each. What is its theoretical maximum number of combinations?
physical-9-q17.e: The theoretical maximum is the number of positions per wheel raised to the number of wheels: 100^3 = 1,000,000. The figure of 100,000,000 corresponds to the book's 4-wheel padlock example, and the p^t formula does not subtract positions already used on other wheels.

physical-9-q18.q: Which of the following is one of the three security problems of master keying identified in the chapter?
o: It creates multiple shear lines, giving more points for surreptitious opening
It forces each user with broad access to carry a different key for every lock
It prevents rearranging locks by means of interchangeable cores
It requires replacing pin tumbler cylinders with simpler warded locks
physical-9-q18.e: The three problems are accountability for master keys, the creation of multiple shear lines or gate openings that make surreptitious opening easier, and increased maintenance because of fragile master pieces. Having each user carry one key per lock is exactly what master keying avoids.

physical-9-q19.q: An electrified exit device configured as fail secure will be installed on a code-required exit. Why can that configuration be acceptable?
o: Because pushing the bar opens the door mechanically, with or without power
Because fail secure locks open by themselves when power is cut off
Because the code accepts pressing a button before pushing the bar as a single action
Because the bar is connected to an alarm that notifies the monitoring center
physical-9-q19.e: A fail secure lock is allowed on the egress route only if free egress is guaranteed regardless of the state of power or controls; the electrified exit device meets this because pushing it opens the door mechanically. Opening when power is cut describes fail safe, and pressing a button does not count as a single action.

physical-9-q20.q: Which set of requirements applies to a delayed egress device on an emergency exit-only door?
o: A 15 or 30 s delay, special signage, connection to the fire alarm and no delay during a fire
A 60 s delay, with no connection to the fire alarm so as not to alert the person trying to leave
A 15 or 30 s delay that is maintained even during a fire alarm or a general evacuation
A delay long enough for an officer to always intercept the thief before the door can be opened
physical-9-q20.e: Pushing the bar starts a 15 or 30 second delay; the device requires signage warning of the delay, connection to the fire alarm system and no delay during a fire or other defined life safety emergency. It usually does not give time to intercept a thief, but it triggers a local alarm and reports it to a monitoring center.

physical-9-q21.q: While auditing a site's locking system, the manager finds that no one knows for certain who has access to what and that there are no distinct access levels. According to the chapter's quick test, how is the system rated?
o: It is neither secure nor convenient, and because of both it is not economical either
It is secure but not convenient, because a single access level simplifies control
It is convenient but not secure, and still economical because it uses few keys
It only has a privacy problem, which is fixed by adding locks as they are needed
physical-9-q21.e: If it is not clear who accesses what, the system is not secure; if there are not several access levels, it is not convenient; and with both failures it is not economical, because money is misapplied. Adding or removing locks 'as needed' is not a locking concept: the system is designed, not merely installed.

physical-9-q22.q: According to Purpura (2013), what are the three security purposes of lighting?
o: Psychological deterrence, enabling detection and enhancing video surveillance
Deterrence, delaying the intruder and reducing legal liability
Detection, recognition and identification of people at a distance
Distinguishing public from private space, supporting response and reducing costs
physical-9-q22.e: The three purposes are psychological deterrence, enabling detection and enhancing video surveillance. Distinguishing public from private space, supporting response or reducing liability appear among the general benefits of lighting, and detection, recognition and identification are the tasks in the reflected-light rule of thumb.

physical-9-q23.q: To 'harden' a parking lot, a manager installs very powerful floodlights that leave very bright areas next to dark ones. What is the MOST likely effect according to the chapter?
o: Less security: the extreme contrast creates black zones where people hide and cameras cannot see
More security, because more light always improves intruder detection and the quality of video images
More security, because glare affects the intruder but never the officers or the cameras
No significant effect, because the human eye adapts instantly to abrupt changes in lighting
physical-9-q23.e: Over-lighting and glare reduce security: the extreme contrast creates black zones where people hide, cameras cannot see and staff cannot observe, and the eye needs 20 to 60 seconds to refocus after glare. More light is not necessarily better.

physical-9-q24.q: A standard camera must allow identification of people crossing a pedestrian entrance at night. According to the chapter's rule of thumb, what minimum level of reflected light is needed?
o: 2.0 fc
1.0 fc
0.5 fc
0.2 fc
physical-9-q24.e: The rule of thumb calls for 0.5 fc (foot-candles) for detection, 1.0 fc for recognition and 2.0 fc for identification. The 0.2 fc value is the one the NRC specifies for the perimeter and the clear zone between fences.

physical-9-q25.q: When comparing lamp technologies for a large parking lot, which factor should weigh MOST in operating cost, according to the chapter?
o: Efficacy in lumens per watt, because energy is about 88% of the cost
The price of lamps and ballasts, because capital goods are about 88% of the cost
Cleaning and replacement labor, because maintenance is about 88% of the cost
Uniformity of distribution, because energy is only about 8% of the total cost
physical-9-q25.e: Energy represents about 88% of the cost of operating lighting, compared with 8% for capital goods and 4% for maintenance; that is why the most important factor is lamp efficacy, that is, lumens emitted per watt consumed.

physical-9-q26.q: A site will use color cameras to identify the color of vehicles and clothing in an outdoor yard. According to Figure 9.25 on the color rendering index (CRI), which light source is MOST suitable?
o: LED
Mercury vapor
High-pressure sodium
Low-pressure sodium
physical-9-q26.e: LED has a CRI of 75 to 90, while mercury vapor has 50, high-pressure sodium 20 and low-pressure sodium 5. Those three have very low CRI and should not be used with color cameras or where color identification is critical; under low-pressure sodium, for example, a green shirt looks bluish.

physical-9-q27.q: In a store's checkout area, the metal halide fixtures go out because of a brief voltage dip. What should the security professional anticipate?
o: That restrike may take up to about 20 minutes, so backup from batteries, a generator or a UPS is advisable
That they will relight instantly as soon as voltage returns, just like the store's LED and incandescent lamps
That they will be slow to reach full output only in very cold weather, as happens mainly with fluorescent lamps
That the real cause is dirt accumulated on the fixture, which cuts its output by about 20% a year in dirty settings
physical-9-q27.e: HID (high-intensity discharge) lamps such as metal halide depend on an arc that goes out if voltage drops, and the tube must cool before it can restrike: this can take up to 20 minutes. In high-security or life safety areas, such as cash registers, batteries, generators or a UPS should be considered.

physical-10-q0.q: Under Crowe's (1991) classification of CPTED (Crime Prevention Through Environmental Design) measures, which of these examples is a natural measure?
o: Walls and gates integrated into the site layout
Chain-link fencing installed along the perimeter
Police patrols and a neighborhood watch program
CCTV cameras connected to a monitoring center
physical-10-q0.e: Crowe classifies terrain, layout, landscaping, gates and walls as natural measures. Note that fencing appears among the mechanical measures, together with locks and CCTV, while patrols and neighborhood watch are organizational measures.

physical-10-q1.q: In an office complex, graffiti, trash and abandoned furniture are piling up, and a car with a broken window has been parked for weeks. Which CPTED tool MOST directly addresses this situation?
o: Management and maintenance, based on the broken windows theory
Legitimate activity support, with a police substation on the premises
Natural access control, with thorny shrubs beneath the low windows
Natural territorial reinforcement, with low hedges marking each property
physical-10-q1.e: According to the broken windows theory (Wilson and Kelling, 1982), unrepaired deterioration gives the impression of abandonment and of the absence of a capable guardian, which increases criminal opportunity; the answer is to maintain and repair the space. Legitimate activity support is for reclaiming places that are hard to protect because of their location or geography.

physical-10-q2.q: Which three objectives define situational crime prevention?
o: Increasing the offender's effort, increasing the offender's risk and reducing the perceived reward
Deterring, detecting and delaying the offender, and also denying access to the target
Reinforcing territoriality, surveillance and access control of the place
Improving cohesion, community culture and connectivity of the neighborhood
physical-10-q2.e: Situational crime prevention manages, designs or manipulates the environment systematically and as permanently as possible to increase the offender's effort and risk and reduce the perceived reward. The other options correspond to the 4 Ds, the three elements of CPTED and second generation CPTED strategies.

physical-10-q3.q: In a neighborhood, an excess of abandoned properties is starting to tip the area toward crime, and a program seeks to balance legitimate commerce, recreation and diverse housing. Which second generation CPTED strategy applies?
o: Capacity threshold, also called tipping point theory
Cohesion, through neighborhood associations and personal development
Connectivity, with political support from higher levels of government
Community culture, through artistic and sports activities
physical-10-q3.e: According to Saville and Cleveland (2013), capacity threshold (tipping point theory) balances land uses and urban elements: too many abandoned properties tip the area toward crime, and a balance of commerce, recreation and diverse housing improves livability. Cohesion works with groups and personal skills, not with the mix of land uses.

physical-10-q4.q: While evaluating a space with the CPTED 3-D tool, a consultant asks: 'Is its ownership clear? Where are its boundaries? Do signs indicate the limits of access?' Which factor do these questions belong to?
o: Definition
Designation
Design
Deterrence
physical-10-q4.e: The definition factor asks how the space is defined, whether its ownership is clear, where its boundaries are and whether signs indicate the proper use or the limits of access. Designation deals with the purpose of the space, and design with whether the physical form supports the intended function and behaviors.

physical-10-q5.q: An apartment was burglarized: the door jamb was damaged and an exterior light is burned out. To prevent repeat victimization, what should management do FIRST?
o: Quickly remove the signs of the burglary: repair the jamb, change locks and keys and replace the light
Regulate access to the building by requiring credentials or permits from everyone who wants to enter
Protect vulnerable targets with roll-down gates and fences that deny access after hours
Block easy access by relocating valuable property to a less exposed place in the building
physical-10-q5.e: The first step against repeat victimization is to quickly remove the signs of victimization: in apartments, replace glass, repair door jambs, change locks and keys and repair broken or burned-out lights. Blocking easy access, protecting vulnerable targets and regulating access are later steps in the same sequence.

physical-10-q6.q: A company has just commissioned an architect for its new headquarters. In which phase of the traditional building planning process should security needs be addressed?
o: Programming, when the owner explains the building's purpose and its occupants
Schematic design, when the architect draws the bubble diagrams of the building
Design development, when the drawings add engineering detail and a larger scale
Construction documents, when the final technical specifications are set
physical-10-q6.e: Security must be addressed in the programming phase, when the owner tells the architect the building's purpose and its occupants. Once the architect has set circulation, access, materials and fenestration, every security change requires modifying drawings and specifications, with more time and money.

physical-10-q7.q: When applying security zoning to a corporate building, how does the chapter classify the employee dining room and the loading dock?
o: Both are controlled zones
Both are unrestricted zones
Both are restricted zones
The dining room is unrestricted and the dock is restricted
physical-10-q7.e: Controlled zones require a valid reason to enter and, once inside, allow movement without severe restriction; the book lists administrative offices, employee dining rooms, security offices and loading docks there. Unrestricted zones are lobbies, reception areas and snack bars; restricted zones are vaults, mechanical areas or laboratories.

physical-10-q8.q: According to the chapter, what is the MOST basic tool for reinforcing territoriality among a building's users?
o: A good training and awareness program
Signage with clear rules in all critical areas of the building
Real fences and walls that clearly mark the property boundaries
Visible video surveillance at entrances, corridors and parking areas
physical-10-q8.e: The most basic tool is a good training and awareness program: people know what to look for and feel empowered to participate. Signage is the simple tool that communicates the designated use of the environment, but it is not the most basic one.

physical-10-q9.q: A manager posts 'Enter at own risk' and 'Lock your valuables' signs in a parking lot. What legal effect does the chapter attribute to that signage?
o: It shifts part of the responsibility to users who do not comply, but it does not relieve the owner of liability
It relieves the owner of all liability as long as the sign is visible and well lighted
It has no effect at all, because user behavior is always left to personal interpretation
It makes any future crime no longer foreseeable for the owner of the property
physical-10-q9.e: Signs put users on notice and attempt to shift part of the responsibility to them: if they break clear rules, the burden passes to them. However, posting a sign does not relieve the building owner of liability; and it is the absence of notice, not the sign, that leaves behavior to personal interpretation.

physical-10-q10.q: A landscape designer proposes a design for the walkways of a corporate park. Which combination complies with the chapter's rules for secure landscaping?
o: Low shrubs no taller than 32 in (81 cm) and tree canopies limbed up to 8 ft (2.4 m)
Low shrubs no taller than 4 ft (1.2 m) and tree canopies limbed up to 5 ft (1.5 m)
Low shrubs no taller than 32 in (81 cm) and loose gravel as ground cover along the paths
Solid 6 ft (1.8 m) hedges along the path to provide privacy and mark the territory
physical-10-q10.e: The rules set a maximum of 32 in for low shrubs, set back 1 yd from the edge of the path, and limbing tree canopies up to 8 ft, to keep sightlines clear and reduce hiding places. Hard landscaping must not include loose gravel or pavers that can serve as projectiles.

physical-10-q11.q: In the architectural program for a corporate office, where should conference rooms used by outside visitors be located?
o: Outside the restricted zone, next to the lobby and before the access control point
Inside the restricted zone, next to the executive offices, so attendees can be supervised
Next to the computer room, to make presentations requiring sensitive equipment easier
On a VIP floor with an exclusive elevator and access control in the elevator itself
physical-10-q11.e: Conference rooms belong outside the restricted zone, normally next to the lobby and before the access control point; that way attendees do not need to be issued badges and are kept out of private or semiprivate areas.

physical-10-q12.q: An industrial plant has a 12 x 12 in (30 x 30 cm) ventilation grille 10 ft (3 m) above the ground. According to the chapter, what is the proper action?
o: Reinforce it, because it exceeds 96 sq in (619 cm2) and is less than 18 ft (5.5 m) above the ground
Leave it as is, because any opening more than 8 ft (2.4 m) above the ground is out of reach
Leave it as is, because it is smaller than 96 sq in (619 cm2) and no person can pass through
Eliminate it, because every opening less than 18 ft (5.5 m) above the ground is prohibited in the shell
physical-10-q12.e: Every opening larger than 96 sq in (619 cm2) that is less than 18 ft above the ground must be reinforced with polycarbonate, window sheets, mesh or similar. The grille measures 144 sq in and is at 10 ft, so it meets both conditions; the rule calls for reinforcement, not elimination.

physical-10-q13.q: Traffic engineers prefer multiple entrances to a parking facility. From a CPTED standpoint, what is preferred, and what is required if volume makes more entrances necessary?
o: A single entrance and exit; each extra access point needs an attended booth, gate arm, shutter, video and good lighting
Multiple entrances to spread the traffic; it is enough for each to have video and good night lighting
A single entrance with several exit-only doors, with no need for attended booths at any of them
Two separate access points, one for vehicles and one for pedestrians that crosses the vehicle lane by the booth
physical-10-q13.e: CPTED prefers a single entrance and exit for all vehicles, because more entrances make it harder to control users and uses. If volume requires more, each access point needs an attended booth, a gate arm, a roll-down shutter to close after hours, video and good lighting; in addition, the primary rule is not to force pedestrians to cross the vehicle path.

physical-10-q14.q: To save money, a bank proposes installing only dummy cameras at an isolated ATM. What is the security professional's BEST response?
o: Reject it: without real cameras, dummies create an illusion of security and a risk of a negligence lawsuit
Accept it, because visible cameras deter more than hidden ones, even though they suffer more vandalism
Accept it if daily withdrawal limits are also set to reduce the loss in case a customer is robbed
Accept it if the dummy cameras are installed inside dark, vandal-resistant polycarbonate domes
physical-10-q14.e: Dummy cameras should be used only if real cameras are also present; otherwise they provide false security and expose the operator to a negligence lawsuit for creating an 'illusion of security'. Visible cameras do deter more, but that does not justify having none that record.

physical-10-q15.q: Which set of typical minimum lighting levels for an ATM, measured 3 ft (1 m) above the ground, does the chapter give?
o: 25 fc (269 lux) at the face; 10 fc within 5 ft (1.5 m); 2 fc at 50 to 60 ft (15 to 18 m)
10 fc (107 lux) at the face; 5 fc within 5 ft (1.5 m); 2 fc at 50 to 60 ft (15 to 18 m)
25 fc (269 lux) at the face; 2 fc within 5 ft (1.5 m); 10 fc at 50 to 60 ft (15 to 18 m)
50 fc (538 lux) at the face; 25 fc within 5 ft (1.5 m); 10 fc at 50 to 60 ft (15 to 18 m)
physical-10-q15.e: The typical minimums are 25 fc (foot-candles) at the face of the ATM, 10 fc within 5 ft and 2 fc at 50 to 60 ft, measured 3 ft above the ground. The chapter notes that the U.S. has no national bank lighting standards and that these minimums do not address shadows, glare or uniformity.

physical-10-q16.q: When designing a new U.S. federal building against bomb attacks, which combination of measures follows the chapter's recommendations?
o: A 100 ft (30 m) setback, a simple rectangular plan and concrete planters spaced less than 4 ft (1.2 m) apart
A 100 ft (30 m) setback, a U-shaped plan enclosing a courtyard and heavy exterior cladding against the blast
A 30 ft (9 m) setback, an L-shaped plan and concrete planters spaced about 6 ft (1.8 m) apart
Vehicle approaches perpendicular to the facade and open parking underneath the building itself
physical-10-q16.e: The chapter recommends a secure perimeter as far out as possible, with a 100 ft setback, and barriers disguised as planters spaced less than 4 ft apart to stop vehicles. A simple rectangular plan reduces the diffraction of the blast wave that bounces around U- or L-shaped buildings, and exterior cladding should be lightweight.

physical-10-q17.q: Which statement BEST describes the relationship between CPTED and traditional security, according to the chapter?
o: It is rarely sufficient alone, but it is a cost-effective complement that can reduce guards and insurance premiums
In most cases it replaces traditional security, because its natural means have no cost
It only works against common crime, since it never reduces the opportunity for a terrorist attack
It makes protection more expensive, because it requires adding guards and expanding the reach of video systems
physical-10-q17.e: Only in rare cases is CPTED sufficient by itself; it is an excellent, cost-effective complement that can reduce or reassign guards, reduce the scope of video, replace some barriers with natural access control and lower insurance premiums. It is also a legitimate strategy for reducing the opportunity for terrorism, although it may not stop the most determined terrorist.

physical-11-q0.q: After several intrusions, the security manager tunes a laboratory's biometric reader to minimize false accepts. What is the MOST likely effect of this adjustment?
o: Type I errors (false rejects) will increase, and authorized users will sometimes be denied entry.
Type I and Type II errors will both fall, because a strict threshold improves overall accuracy.
The device will lock onto the equal error rate, where both error types are at their lowest.
Type II errors will increase, and authorized users will sometimes be denied entry.
physical-11-q0.e: Both errors cannot be minimized at once: tuning for few false accepts gives high security but raises false rejects (Type I), so some authorized users are denied. The equal error rate is used to compare devices; it is not the point where both errors are lowest.

physical-11-q1.q: A high-security company wants to install electromagnetic locks (maglocks) on its designated egress doors and add battery backup so they stay locked during a power outage. What should the security manager recommend?
o: Wire them fail-safe, tied to the fire alarm, with no battery backup and with prior AHJ approval.
Accept the battery backup, since the book recommends it for maglocks in high-security facilities.
Configure them as fail-secure so the door stays locked after any power or control failure.
Replace them with electric deadbolts, which can be fail-secure and do not rely on an electromagnet.
physical-11-q1.e: On an egress door a maglock must be fail-safe, release with the fire alarm and be approved by the AHJ; per the book, adding battery backup to a maglock is a crime in most jurisdictions. The backup power the book recommends for high security excludes egress doors, and electric deadbolts are not recommended on doors that must open on a fire alarm.

physical-11-q2.q: An access control system creates the duress code by swapping the last two digits of the PIN. An employee is assigned PIN 4-8-3-3. What problem does this PIN create for that scheme?
o: The duress code would be identical to the normal PIN, so the system could not tell them apart.
The duress code would match another employee's PIN, because only the last two digits change.
A four-digit PIN is not enough for a workforce of several hundred people and is easy to guess.
The system would void the credential on first use, treating the PIN as a failed attempt.
physical-11-q2.e: Swapping the last two digits (3-3) yields the same number, which is why the book requires those digits to differ (all four, if the code reverses the PIN). Four digits give 10,000 combinations, enough for a few hundred people.

physical-11-q3.q: What is the MAIN advantage of an exchange badge system over a conventional photo identification badge?
o: The badge used inside the secure area never leaves it, reducing counterfeiting, loss and theft.
It verifies the person's identity by matching a unique physical trait recorded at enrollment.
It prevents an intruder from using makeup or a disguise to resemble the photo on a stolen badge.
It lets the badge be checked automatically at the reader, without relying on an attentive guard.
physical-11-q3.e: The twin badge stays at the control point and the employee's own badge is held there until exit, so the badge used inside never leaves the area. It is still a manual check vulnerable to disguise, and it is not identity verification, which only biometrics provides.

physical-11-q4.q: Which BEST describes a security drawback of master keying that must be weighed against its convenience?
o: It creates additional shear lines that make it easier to open the lock covertly.
It requires reusable cores, which makes replacing lost or stolen keys more expensive.
Split pins greatly increase the number of key changes available in each cylinder.
Each change key opens every lock within its master key group.
physical-11-q4.e: The book cites three difficulties: strict key control, more weak points for manipulation (multiple shear lines or gate openings) and more cylinder maintenance. Split pins reduce key changes, reusable cores make recovering from a lost key cheaper, and a change key opens only one lock.

physical-11-q5.q: Why does the book advise against using a traditional magnetometer to detect contraband?
o: It is passive and senses only ferromagnetic metals, missing copper, aluminum, zinc and composites.
It emits a pulsed magnetic field that causes nuisance alarms whenever steel beams or rebar are nearby.
It relies on ionizing radiation, so it is not considered safe for screening people at an entry point.
It responds only to low atomic number (low-Z) materials and therefore does not react to steel weapons.
physical-11-q5.e: A magnetometer is passive: it monitors the earth's magnetic field and detects only changes caused by ferromagnetic materials, so it misses copper, aluminum, zinc and many composite weapons. Pulsed fields belong to modern active detectors, and ionizing radiation to X-ray systems.

physical-11-q6.q: At a checkpoint, screeners must look for explosive traces inside containers and in soft-sided fabric bags, as unobtrusively as possible. Which technique is MOST appropriate?
o: Vapor sampling: drawing in the air next to the item, often while agitating it.
Swipe sampling: wiping a cloth swab across the surface and then heating it.
Raman analysis: aiming a laser at the container and analyzing the scattered light.
Computed tomography (CT): rebuilding the contents in 3D to compute mass and density.
physical-11-q6.e: Vapor sampling suits container interiors and soft surfaces and is less invasive because it does not touch the item. Swipe sampling is more efficient and collects more mass but is best for hard surfaces and more invasive; Raman needs small but visible amounts and is not for packages, and CT is bulk, not trace, detection.

physical-11-q7.q: Per the book, which of these alarms is classified as a false alarm rather than as another type of nuisance alarm?
o: An alarm caused by the failure of a component in the sensor itself.
An alarm caused by wind-blown debris moving across the detection zone.
An alarm caused by ground vibration from a train passing nearby.
An alarm caused by a large animal bumping into the fence at night.
physical-11-q7.e: A false alarm is a type of nuisance alarm generated by the equipment itself: poor design, inadequate maintenance or component failure. Wind-blown debris and ground vibration are industrial nuisance sources and animals are natural ones; none of them is caused by an intrusion.

physical-11-q8.q: A designer pairs, in the same sector, a sensor that detects tunneling with another that detects fence climbing, so each covers the other's weaknesses. Which logic should be used, and what will happen to the nuisance alarm rate (NAR)?
o: OR combination; the system NAR will be the sum of the individual sensors' NARs.
AND combination; the system NAR will be lower than that of either sensor.
OR combination; the system NAR will be lower than that of either sensor.
AND combination; the system PD will be the product of the individual sensors' PDs.
physical-11-q8.e: When sensors detect different intrusion types (above ground, overhead and tunneling) they are combined with OR logic, which alarms on any sensor; the resulting NAR is the sum of the individual NARs, so each sensor needs a low NAR. With AND logic the intruder would only need to defeat one sensor to avoid an alarm.

physical-11-q9.q: To protect a high-security classified space, an integrator proposes one dual-technology sensor (microwave plus passive infrared, PIR) per room instead of two separate sensors. How should the security manager respond?
o: Reject it; use separately mounted microwave and PIR units, ideally perpendicular, logically combined.
Accept it, because the AND logic of a dual sensor raises the PD above that of either technology alone.
Accept it if each technology has a PD of 0.95, because the combined unit will also achieve 0.95.
Reject it and use a single multisegment PIR, which is better at detecting motion toward the sensor.
physical-11-q9.e: In high security a single dual sensor is never used in place of two separate sensors, and many government standards do not allow them in a SCIF. With AND logic the PD is the product of both (0.95 x 0.95, about 0.90), lower than either; mounted separately and perpendicular, each sensor exploits its best motion (approach for microwave, crosswalk for PIR).

physical-11-q10.q: In a warehouse, the shelving layout forces any intruder to move directly toward the spot where the motion sensor will be mounted. Considering only the direction of motion, which sensor will perform BEST?
o: A monostatic microwave sensor, which is most sensitive to motion toward or away from it.
A passive infrared (PIR) sensor, which is most sensitive to motion toward or away from it.
A passive infrared (PIR) sensor, whose detection does not depend on the direction of motion.
A monostatic microwave sensor, which is most sensitive to motion that crosses its pattern.
physical-11-q10.e: Microwave sensors detect by Doppler shift and are more sensitive to motion toward or away from the sensor than to crosswalk motion. PIR is the opposite: it performs best with motion that crosses its pattern, because the target must enter and leave several segments.

physical-11-q11.q: In a clear zone bounded by two parallel fences, where are perimeter delay barriers typically placed, and why?
o: At or near the inner fence, so the intruder crosses the detection zone before reaching it.
At the outer fence, so the intruder is slowed down well before entering the detection zone.
In the middle of the clear zone, so the camera sees the intruder while working on the barrier.
Outside the outer fence, to keep people, animals and vehicles well away from the sensors.
physical-11-q11.e: Barriers go at or near the inner fence: the intruder crosses the detection zone first, so the response begins before the delay starts. The barrier also must not degrade sensor performance or block part of the camera's view.

physical-11-q12.q: A designer wants to add complementary sensors to a high-security perimeter. According to the book, which of these pairs would NOT be complementary?
o: Bistatic and monostatic microwave
Bistatic microwave and active infrared
Bistatic microwave and ported coaxial cable
Ported coaxial cable and active infrared
physical-11-q12.e: Complementary sensors must use different technologies with detection patterns that can overlap. Bistatic and monostatic microwave are vulnerable to the same attack methods and the same nuisance alarm sources; the other three pairs are complementary according to the book.

physical-11-q13.q: A UK installer builds an intruder alarm system with a grade 3 panel and sounder but uses grade 2 motion detectors in some zones. Under the European standards, what is the official grade of the system?
o: Grade 2, because the system takes the grade of its lowest-graded equipment.
Grade 3, because the grade is set by the control panel and the signaling path.
Grade 3, because most of the installed equipment is rated grade 3.
No grade, because the European standards forbid mixing equipment of different grades.
physical-11-q13.e: The European standards allow mixing equipment of different grades, but the system's official grade is that of its lowest-graded equipment. Grade 2 detectors therefore bring the whole system down to grade 2.

physical-11-q14.q: What is the MOST important limitation that an assets protection professional must understand about UL standards for alarms and intrusion detection systems?
o: They address safety, not security, and do not assess equipment vulnerability to adversaries.
They apply only to high-security equipment for classified spaces, such as those governed by UL 2050.
They are not public, so the professional must rely on the periodic directories to learn their content.
They set installation rules for European grade 1 to 4 systems but do not cover equipment made in the US.
physical-11-q14.e: UL standards are safety standards: they guide correct installation to reduce fire and similar risks, but they do not address equipment vulnerabilities or the ability to detect malicious adversaries. They are also public; what UL asks is that users rely on its directories of certified equipment.

physical-11-q15.q: During an audit, the security manager finds that the installer placed all end-of-line (EOL) resistors inside the IDS control panel instead of next to each sensor. Why is this a problem?
o: The run between the panel and each sensor is left unsupervised, though line supervision must cover it.
Resistors at the panel cause nuisance alarms from electromagnetic interference from the other circuits.
Line supervision only works with IP network transmitters, so the resistors are unnecessary anyway.
The resistors belong at the central station receiver, not at the panel or out in the field.
physical-11-q15.e: With several sensors on one processor, line supervision is needed between the processor and each sensor; the recommended method is an EOL device placed in the circuit next to the sensor, in the field, not at the panel. That way cuts, shorts or bridging on that run are detected.

physical-11-q16.q: Which BEST describes the advantage of a balanced magnetic switch (BMS) over a simple magnetic switch?
o: Its bias magnet detects changes in field strength, which defeats spoofing with an external magnet.
It is fully electronic, with no mechanical reeds, and measures the field using its own power supply.
It also detects someone cutting through the door leaf, even if the door is never opened.
It alarms on any door separation from the jamb, even one of 0.5 in (1.3 cm) or less.
physical-11-q16.e: A BMS has an adjustable bias magnet and senses changes in field strength, so holding a strong magnet near it, which defeats a simple switch, no longer works. The fully electronic, powered device is the Hall effect switch, and cutting through the door leaf still bypasses a BMS.

physical-11-q17.q: An IP camera must read the license plates of vehicles leaving a parking lot. Based on the book's digital identification views, what minimum pixel density is needed at the point of capture?
o: 70 px/ft (231 px/m)
46 px/ft (150 px/m)
88 px/ft (289 px/m)
35 px/ft (118 px/m)
physical-11-q17.e: License plate identification requires 70 px/ft (231 px/m). 46 px/ft is subject identification beyond a shadow of a doubt, 88 px/ft is facial recognition, and 35 px/ft is recognizing known people.

physical-11-q18.q: A camera is mounted on a building wall 40 ft above the ground, and the center of the scene is 30 ft from the building. What camera-to-scene distance should be used to calculate the lens focal length?
o: 50 ft, the hypotenuse of the mounting height and the horizontal distance
30 ft, the horizontal distance from the building to the scene center
40 ft, the mounting height of the camera above the ground
70 ft, the sum of the camera's mounting height and the horizontal distance
physical-11-q18.e: Distance is measured from the front of the camera to the main subject with the Pythagorean theorem: the square root of (30 squared + 40 squared) = square root of 2,500 = 50 ft. Using only the horizontal distance (30 ft) understates it and leads to the wrong lens.

physical-11-q19.q: For cameras meant to provide visual information about something that is happening or has happened, in what order should the selection criteria be applied, according to the book?
o: Sensitivity, resolution, then features; the camera is chosen before the lens.
Resolution, sensitivity, then features; the lens is chosen before the camera.
Features, resolution, then sensitivity; the camera is selected before the lens.
Sensitivity, features, then resolution; the lens is selected before the camera.
physical-11-q19.e: The book sets the order as sensitivity first (minimum light for a quality image), then resolution, then features, and the camera is chosen before the lens. The lens is the second most important decision, after the camera.

physical-11-q20.q: A technician wants to reuse a C-mount lens on a new CS-mount camera and does not have the adapter ring at hand. What should the manager warn about?
o: Mounting it without the 5 mm spacer can break the camera's CCD.
It will work, but with focus problems that no adjustment can correct.
It will work fine, because CS cameras accept any C-mount lens directly.
It will produce tunnel vision, because the C lens will not fill the CS sensor.
physical-11-q20.e: C-mount has 17.526 mm between sensor and lens and CS-mount 12.5 mm: a C lens on a CS camera without an adapter ring breaks the CCD, while the 5 mm spacer makes it work. Uncorrectable focus problems occur in the reverse case (CS lens on a C camera), and tunnel vision comes from a lens format smaller than the camera's.

physical-11-q21.q: Why does the book consider dummy cameras a liability?
o: They create a false expectation that someone is watching and that help is on the way.
They violate the reasonable expectation of privacy just as a real camera in a restroom would.
They require video surveillance signage to be posted at every entrance to the building.
They make video from real cameras covering the same scene inadmissible as evidence.
physical-11-q21.e: Dummy cameras create an expectation of protection: a person under attack believes they are being watched and that help is coming. Signage at entrances is an accepted legal practice, but it is not something a dummy camera imposes.

physical-11-q22.q: A video surveillance integrator asks to be paid the full contract amount as soon as the cameras are installed. What is MOST advisable to ensure the project is completed to the required performance?
o: Put acceptance tests in the contract terms and withhold final payment until they are passed.
Pay upon installation, then require the equipment to complete a burn-in of a few hundred hours.
Rely on the manufacturer's final factory inspection and on its published performance specifications.
Pay upon installation and order 10 to 20 percent spares to cover any cameras that fail.
physical-11-q22.e: The book recommends requiring acceptance tests from every vendor or integrator, including them in the contract terms and conditions, and withholding final payment until they are passed. Final factory inspection is not consistent, and manufacturer literature should not be the only criterion.

physical-11-q23.q: A facility uses a loop circuit with a McCulloh configuration. An intruder cuts the loop wire at two different points. What happens?
o: Only the devices between the two cuts are lost; all the others keep working.
All devices keep working, because current reaches them from both sides of the circuit.
All devices beyond the first cut are lost, just as in a simple loop circuit.
The whole loop is lost, because a McCulloh circuit tolerates shorts but not cuts.
physical-11-q23.e: A McCulloh circuit sends current from both sides of the loop: with one cut all devices keep working, but with two cuts the devices between them are lost because there is no path to them. In a simple loop, by contrast, one cut interrupts every signal beyond it.

physical-11-q24.q: Which type of alarm transmission installation means a line fault affects only one detector and forces an attacker to find and disable each sensor's cable?
o: Point-to-point, although it costs more than a loop because it needs more cable.
Multiplexing, although cutting the shared link drops every signal carried on it.
Loop, although a cut at the right spot can disable all detectors in an area.
Wireless, although any unencrypted signal must be considered interceptable.
physical-11-q24.e: In point-to-point each sensor has its own wire pair to the control center: a fault affects one detector and an attacker would have to disable every cable. Its drawback is the cost of extra cable; in loop and multiplexed systems a single cut affects many signals.

physical-11-q25.q: While an operator is assessing an alarm on screen, a second alarm arrives. Under the 'operator first' design philosophy, how should the interface behave?
o: Show a non-intrusive notice and let the operator decide whether to abort the current task.
Replace the current screen with the new alarm, since the most recent alarm takes priority.
Sound a loud, continuous alarm until the operator acknowledges the new alarm.
Hold back the new alarm entirely until the operator has finished and closed the current assessment.
physical-11-q25.e: Rule 4 of the 'operator first' approach is not to interrupt operations in progress: the new alarm does not replace the screen; a non-intrusive notification arrives and the operator decides whether to abort. Rule 5 also calls for avoiding loud, continuous alarms.

physical-11-q26.q: According to the book, which combination of voice scrambling techniques provides a high degree of security?
o: Masking combined with a band splitter or with a frequency or phase modulator
A frequency inverter combined with a band splitter using five fixed bands
Masking used alone, with a single tone or RF noise inside the voice band
A five-band band splitter on its own, which offers 3,080 combinations in theory
physical-11-q26.e: Masking alone is weak, because the voice is fairly easy to understand through the mask, and 90 percent of a band splitter's 3,080 combinations are no more secure than an inverter. Combined, masking plus a band splitter or masking plus a frequency or phase modulator gives high security.

physical-11-q27.q: A manufacturer releases smoke detectors that integrate miniature cameras, microphones and inert gas monitoring. Which electronic systems integration trend does this product illustrate?
o: Product hybridization
Data aggregation
Cloud-based managed services
Big data
physical-11-q27.e: Product hybridization merges formerly separate products; the book gives exactly the example of smoke detectors with miniature cameras, microphones and inert gas monitoring. Data aggregation, by contrast, means managing diverse databases from a single interface.

physical-12-q0.q: A security manager is evaluating whether a reception post can be replaced by technology. Under the 'necessary human being' concept, which post requirement BEST justifies keeping a person there?
o: Holding face-to-face dialogue with visitors and deciding the next step from it
Reading access cards and checking them against the authorized cardholder database
Switching on the lobby lighting whenever motion is detected
Locking and unlocking the lobby doors according to a fixed daily schedule
physical-12-q0.e: Engaging in rational face-to-face dialogue and deciding the next step based on it is one of the five capabilities that require a human being. Reading cards, switching on lights or locking doors on a schedule are tasks a reader or an automated system can do without staff.

physical-12-q1.q: An entrance requires personal recognition and has low-density queuing. According to the book, how many entrances can a single remote operator control under these conditions?
o: 1 or 2 entrances
3 or 4 entrances
5 or 6 entrances
8 to 10 entrances
physical-12-q1.e: The book states that, with personal recognition and low-density queuing, one remote operator can control 3 or 4 entrances. It illustrates how technology lets an organization use people only where human capabilities are needed, rather than placing an officer at every door.

physical-12-q2.q: A company decides to have contract officers work side by side with its proprietary officers to gain operational control and reduce administrative burden. What must it review BEFORE implementing this model?
o: The applicable co-employment rules
The bid specifications from the previous contract
The use-of-force policy of both groups
The state regulator's uniform requirements
physical-12-q2.e: This is the hybrid model, and the drawback the book notes is that co-employment rules must be reviewed before implementing it. Bid specifications protect quality when buying contract security, but they are not the prerequisite specific to the hybrid model.

physical-12-q3.q: When buying contract security, why does the book warn against deciding on the lowest bid alone?
o: The largest cost component is the officer's wage, so cutting price usually cuts wages and quality
The lowest bid always shifts all of the contractor's legal liability onto the client organization
The largest cost component is equipment, so cutting price forces the use of obsolete equipment
Low-price agencies are unable to meet co-employment rules or the state licensing requirements for officers
physical-12-q3.e: The officer's wage is the largest cost component, so cutting the price usually cuts wages and, with them, quality. That is why the client must write detailed bid specifications covering requirements, wages, benefits and performance expectations; equipment is not the main cost.

physical-12-q4.q: An officer finds a disoriented, agitated person in the lobby who could hurt himself or others. According to the book, how should the officer treat this situation?
o: As a medical emergency: secure the person and the scene, call EMS and keep custody until handover
As a police matter: detain the person and call the police to arrest and remove the individual
As an intoxication case: determine which substance was taken before calling emergency medical services
As a disciplinary matter: identify the person and report the case to human resources after the shift
physical-12-q4.e: A person with altered mental status is a medical emergency, not a police problem: the officer secures the person and the scene, calls emergency medical services (EMS) and keeps custody until handover. The officer is not qualified to determine the cause; only a physician can do that.

physical-12-q5.q: A bomb threat is received against a specific floor of an office building, and management opts for a partial evacuation. Based on the book's example, which floors should it concentrate on in addition to the threatened floor?
o: The floors immediately above and below
All of the floors above the threatened one
The ground floor and the basement levels
The floors with the largest number of occupants
physical-12-q5.e: The book's example of partial evacuation for a bomb threat on a specific floor is to concentrate on the floors immediately above and below. The other options do not match the criterion the book gives.

physical-12-q6.q: An officer assigned to a fixed access control post is asked to accompany a visitor to a conference room on another floor. What is MOST appropriate according to the book?
o: Have the host who invited the visitor, or a non-static post officer, escort
Have the officer escort the visitor and close the post until returning
Have the officer escort the visitor after notifying the control center by radio
Let the visitor go up alone after leaving identification at the post
physical-12-q6.e: A fixed-post officer should not escort visitors or customers, because doing so abandons the protection task; the alternative is an escort by the host or by a non-static post officer. Notifying the control center does not solve the problem of leaving the post unattended.

physical-12-q7.q: Post orders require an hourly vehicle count at a gate. In which record should the evidence that the count was reported to the control center and received be kept?
o: The main or control log, covering significant events at all posts
The post log, which is the chronological, local record of that single post
The special orders issued for the period during which the count is taken
The training log sheet of the officer who performed the count
physical-12-q7.e: The count itself goes in the post log, the chronological, local record of a single post; the evidence that it was reported and received goes in the main or control log, the cumulative and consecutive history of significant events at all posts. Confusing the two logs is the typical trap.

physical-12-q8.q: Reviewing logs, a manager sees that an officer writes every day: 'Arrived 0700. Nothing to report. Relieved 1500.' What is the BEST corrective measure according to the book?
o: Have post orders require logging specific events such as key sign-outs and escorts
Eliminate the post at once, since several uneventful days prove the post is unnecessary
Replace the paper log with an electronic log that has customized and mandatory data fields
Ask the officer to rewrite the earlier log entries with more descriptive detail
physical-12-q8.e: That pattern suggests the post is unnecessary, the officer is not performing, or the officer was not trained to report; so post orders should require recording specific events (keys, escorts, help to visitors or contractors). Eliminating the post jumps to only one of the three explanations, and rewriting entries breaks the rule against altering the log.

physical-12-q9.q: Retail theft ring activity is detected at a shopping mall. Which officer role becomes more important, and what training does it require?
o: Information collection; investigation basics, interviewing and investigative reports
Public relations; corporate expectations and culture, and dealing with the news media
Legal consultant; torts, negligence, contracts, and labor and regulatory law
Physical security specialist; technical aspects of equipment and a lifelong learning effort
physical-12-q9.e: The information collection role grows when organized crime is present, such as retail theft rings, and requires investigative fundamentals, interviewing techniques and investigative report writing. The physical security specialist advises on protection and prevention, but that role is not focused on detecting and reporting criminal activity.

physical-12-q10.q: Where regulations allow it, under which condition does the book justify arming officers with firearms?
o: When it is reasonable to expect the officer will have to use lethal force
When the client wants to project a more authoritative image
When the officer already owns a personal firearm with a valid license
When the firearm makes it possible to cut the site's insurance and training costs
physical-12-q10.e: Arming is justified only if there is greater danger to life without the weapon or if it is reasonable to expect the officer will have to use lethal force. Arming increases, rather than reduces, liability and the costs of training, insurance and regulatory compliance.

physical-12-q11.q: A hospital officer must choose which less than lethal tool to carry in an emergency room that is usually crowded. Which does the book consider irresponsible in that setting?
o: Aerosol irritants (pepper spray), because of their greater residual risk to third parties
Handcuffs, because they are technically not considered self-defense weapons
A stun baton, because it requires direct contact and may cause pain without incapacitating
An expandable baton, because it may only be used on large muscle masses
physical-12-q11.e: Aerosol irritants carry greater residual risk to third parties, and the book cites a crowded emergency room as an example of irresponsible use; they also require aftercare and custody. The limits of batons and stun batons are real, but the book does not present them as unsuitable for that location.

physical-12-q12.q: Under Section 5.3 (Selection of Personnel) of the ASIS Private Security Officer Selection and Training Guideline (PSO), what should the organization do with a candidate whose competence does not meet the post's minimum criteria?
o: Reject the candidate or provide the training needed to meet the criteria
Hire the candidate on probation and evaluate after one year on the job
Assign the candidate only to fixed posts, where supervision is more direct
Lower the post criteria to match what the labor market can supply
physical-12-q12.e: The PSO calls for setting minimum criteria consistent with legal, regulatory and contractual obligations, assessing each person against them, and rejecting anyone who does not meet them or providing the necessary training. Lowering the criteria defeats the purpose of setting minimum standards.

physical-12-q13.q: Which factor of officer behavior must be emphasized in training and consists of acting without haste or excessive emotion, avoiding abusive language, arguments and, if possible, force?
o: Courtesy
Restraint
Interest
Discipline
physical-12-q13.e: Restraint is the factor the book says must be emphasized in training: calm, dignified conduct, tolerance of other opinions, and avoiding arguments and, where possible, force. Courtesy is showing consideration for others, and discipline is a character trait (obeying orders and not leaving the post), not a behavior factor.

physical-12-q14.q: A new training manager must identify the training requirements for a site's officers. According to the book, which source should be reviewed FIRST?
o: Legal requirements: state statute, regulations, and client and union contracts
Training guidelines published by ASIS International, NASCO and the IACP for officers
Training calendars of similar facilities in the same area
Priorities identified by the officers themselves in a job task analysis
physical-12-q14.e: The first step is to identify legal requirements (state statute, administrative rules, client contracts and union contracts; insurers may also impose requirements); standards, guidelines and best practices such as those of ASIS, NASCO and the IACP come next. Community standards and a job task analysis with the officers are complementary sources.

physical-12-q15.q: A manager wants to train officers in use of force and ethics, topics that require discretionary judgment. Which method is MOST appropriate according to the book?
o: Job aids posted at each post
Case studies with active group discussion
A long lecture supported by slides
On-the-job training (OJT) with a checklist
physical-12-q15.e: The case study method, created at Harvard in the 1880s, is useful where discretionary judgment is required (crisis management, use of force and ethics) and works best in groups with active discussion. Job aids only supplement training, and a lecture is ineffective unless it is short and dynamic.

physical-12-q16.q: What distinguishes a field training officer (FTO) program from a mentoring program?
o: The FTO only teaches; the mentor evaluates and may recommend retention or dismissal
The FTO also evaluates and may recommend retention or dismissal; the mentor only teaches
The FTO acts only before assignment; the mentor acts once the officer is on the post
The FTO is simpler to implement; mentoring requires planning and training of the guide
physical-12-q16.e: In an FTO program the guide is also a supervisor who evaluates performance and at some point recommends retention or dismissal; the mentor teaches but neither evaluates nor decides. That is why the FTO role is complex and requires planning, and the book considers mentoring to work better in most security environments.

physical-12-q17.q: A program aims to have officers understand other cultures, deal appropriately with people with disabilities, and grasp the criminal mindset and the speed of an attack. Which learning domain does it mainly address?
o: The cognitive domain
The psychomotor domain
The affective domain
Formal socialization
physical-12-q17.e: The affective domain changes how a person views a situation (attitudes and perception): understanding other cultures, dealing with people with disabilities and grasping the criminal mindset. The cognitive domain focuses on knowledge and theory, and the psychomotor domain on physical skills that require repetition.

physical-12-q18.q: A manager decides to write every lesson plan and teach every course personally; on seeing the workload, he gives up and training stops. Which obstacle to training does the book associate with this 'Frog Syndrome'?
o: Budgetary limitations
Lack of management expertise
Stereotypes of the officer
The manager's ego
physical-12-q18.e: Hertig (1993) called 'Frog Syndrome' the manager who 'jumps in' to train everyone personally and 'jumps out' on seeing the workload; the book places it under the ego obstacle. Lack of management expertise is a separate obstacle: not knowing how to assess needs, write objectives or design tests.

physical-12-q19.q: According to the book, why is 'experience is the best teacher' not necessarily true for an officer's development?
o: It only helps if it is preceded by a university degree in security
It replaces training but never replaces formal education
It must be guided; if misunderstood, wrong lessons are learned
It only counts when validated by an independent inspector
physical-12-q19.e: The book sums it up as Education + Training + Guided Experience = Development. Supervisors and managers must guide experience so that it is formative; if it is not understood, wrong lessons are learned and then repeated.

physical-12-q20.q: Because of construction, a door will be closed for three weeks, which changes the duties of a nearby post. Which type of order applies, and what must it clearly state?
o: A general order applicable to the entire force
A special order stating its period of validity
A permanent post order replacing the previous one
A verbal instruction from the supervisor at shift change
physical-12-q20.e: Special orders address temporary events, such as the temporary closure of another gate that affects a post, and must clearly specify the period in which they are in effect. General orders apply to the entire force, and word-of-mouth instructions are exactly what written orders are meant to avoid.

physical-12-q21.q: At a plant, the first shift runs 0700 to 1500 and the second 1500 to 2300. Management needs more officers during the plant's shift change without paying overtime. What measure does the book propose?
o: Ask two first-shift officers to stay one extra hour, paid as overtime
Have the supervisor regularly cover a fixed post during each plant shift change
Add a one-hour meal to the first shift, making it 0700-1600 to overlap the second
Move the second shift's start to 1400 and pay each officer for the extra hour worked
physical-12-q21.e: Maximizing the straight time schedule means planned shift overlap: a one-hour meal within the shift extends presence to 0700-1600, so from 1500 to 1600 both full shifts are on duty without overtime. Having the supervisor regularly do an officer's work can trigger a grievance where there is a collective bargaining agreement.

physical-12-q22.q: A contract security company wants to test how an officer reacts to a suspicious package brought into the facility. Who should conduct the test according to the book?
o: The officer's immediate supervisor, who knows the post best
The client's manager, so that the test has contractual validity
A fellow officer on the same shift, to make the test more realistic
An independent inspector outside the force's chain of command
physical-12-q22.e: Independent inspectors offer three advantages: the officer does not know them, they are more objective, and they allow better reaction tests, such as introducing a suspicious package. The immediate supervisor may be influenced by personal bias, and the officer would recognize him.

physical-12-q23.q: In the Prince William County (Virginia) Police Business Watch program, which is one of the requirements for an organization to become a Certified Crime Prevention Business?
o: Hire at least one proprietary security officer on every operating shift
Install video surveillance linked to the county police department's dispatch center
Accept an on-site security assessment by personnel knowledgeable in CPTED
Have its security manager join IASIR or a similar association
physical-12-q23.e: The four requirements are written policies and procedures addressing crime, training employees in crime prevention, accepting an on-site assessment by Crime Prevention Unit personnel knowledgeable in CPTED (Crime Prevention Through Environmental Design), and designating a liaison with the police. The program leverages non-security personnel, so it does not require hiring officers.

physical-13-q0.q: In a new building project, the CFO and the building committee control scope and funding; the security manager contributes needs but neither decides nor manages the budget. According to the book, what role does the security manager play in that project?
o: Project influencer
Project stakeholder
Funding controller
Principal decision maker
physical-13-q0.e: The book assigns the security manager the project stakeholder role when others control scope and funds. As a project influencer (along with chief legal counsel or a consultant), the security manager would influence scope and budget, which is not the situation described.

physical-13-q1.q: According to the list of process areas cited in the book (Project Management Institute), to which area do the source selection and contract closeout subprocesses belong?
o: Project integration management
Project communications management
Project procurement management
Project risk management
physical-13-q1.e: Source selection and contract closeout are subprocesses of project procurement management, along with procurement planning, solicitation planning, solicitation and contract administration. The most tempting distractor is communications management, which includes administrative closure, not contract closeout.

physical-13-q2.q: A CEO wants to improve visitor security and asks the security manager to start pricing cameras and readers immediately. What should the manager do FIRST according to the chapter?
o: Issue a request for proposal (RFP) to qualified bidders
Base the project on a security risk assessment
Set the preliminary budget using quotes from several vendors
Call the kick-off meeting with the contractor
physical-13-q2.e: Every security project must be based on a security risk assessment; without it, scope is decided without knowing threats, probabilities, vulnerabilities or consequences, relying only on assumptions. Pricing, bidding or kicking off with a contractor are later steps that depend on that scope.

physical-13-q3.q: Acceptance testing for a physical protection system (PPS) is scheduled for June 30. Following the chapter's process, when should system monitoring training be delivered?
o: Around May 31, about 30 days before testing
Around June 23, one week before testing
On June 30, together with acceptance testing itself
In July, when the 12-month warranty period starts
physical-13-q3.e: The book places system monitoring training 30 days before acceptance testing, as part of managing implementation. One week is the timing of a different event: the bidder's conference or site visit, held one week after the RFP is issued.

physical-13-q4.q: According to the chapter, when a security project exceeds any of its constraints (scope, schedule, budget or quality), what is the usual cause?
o: New threats that emerge during construction
Changes in the applicable codes and regulations
Poor conception or poor project management
Contractor default during the warranty period
